Country of Publication: India Title: Varuṇapaddhativyākhyā (Commentary on the Varuṇapaddhati)
With the commentary *Vilocana* by Ṇigamajñāna (Ṭ.
An Explanation of the Varuṇa-paddhati
I bow to the auspicious Kalpaka-Vināyaka, who is swarmed by bees hovering over the ichor flowing from his temples at all times.
I take refuge in the lotus feet of Naṭarāja, who dances while bestowing his eyes upon Vyāghrapāda and Padmañjali.
May the Goddess, the beloved of Śiva’s desires, who delights Naṭeśvara with the playful movement of her own sidelong glances, grant eternal auspiciousness.
Having paid homage to the Guru and the Goddess of Speech,
this "Eye," which always delights through the *Śrīmad-Varuṇa-paddhati*, is proclaimed by me.
A brief explanation has been stated by my teacher, who spoke according to the words of Śiva; following that, I shall speak concisely and with logical reasoning.
Now, there was a certain teacher named Varuṇa, a knower of the secrets of the Śiva-āgamas.

With a mind purified by the stainless knowledge of the supreme [Vedic] tradition, desiring to speak of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)— which are the seeds and the very essence for the swift destruction of the mental afflictions of all people— he first paid homage to his chosen deity and, following the conduct of the virtuous, commenced the work he had intended to undertake.
He makes this declaration: "Homage to Soma, the source of bliss, who is the seed of the two types of Nirvāṇa. Now, the two seeds for initiation (dīkṣā) and installation (pratiṣṭhā) are summarized."

Salutations to the one who is the seed of the two types of *nirvāṇa*, the cause of the pair of supreme goals (*niḥśreyasa*) consisting of the departure from and the destruction of the bonds such as impurities (*mala*), and who is the source (*yoni*) because he brings forth the fragrance of the former [state] even while in the state of existence (*bhava*). [The suffix] *luṭ* is used here in the sense of existence.
Liberation (*mukti*) is [called] *kaivalya*, *nirvāṇa*, *śreya*, *niḥśreyasa*, and *amṛta*. Cause (*hetu*),
reason (*kāraṇa*), and seed (*bīja*) are synonyms.
Cāmara: To the question "Of what kind is its causality?", he says: "To Soma," that is, to him accompanied by Umā;
by the word "Umā," it is intended that the Śakti who is intent upon bestowing grace upon men, and [the causality belongs] to him alone when accompanied by her.
Because it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

And that power, being twofold—distinguished as being without a substratum (*niradhikaraṇa*) and with a substratum (*sādhikaraṇa*)—is the cause of the two types of *nirvāṇa*. Thus, there is a twofold nature of grace (*anugraha*).
Thus it is stated that there are two kinds of divine nirvāṇa. For this very reason, *śam* means happiness;
because liberation arises from him, he is *Śambhu*. To that Śiva, salutations (*namaḥ*).
By this, it is shown that he alone is worthy of salutation, and no other.

It has been indicated that this is because [those paths] lack the quality of delivering one from conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*). As it has been said: "Those who worship for the sake of liberation while abandoning the Lord (*Īśāna*) together with Ambā are overtaken by the great darkness; for them there is no supreme state."
"Those who, having abandoned the Lord Sāmba, worship another deity,
fall into the most terrible cycle of existence, utterly deluded. Now,
following the salutation to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), by this [verse] the author begins the work with the chosen deity.

The necessity of the auspicious rite consisting of prostration is indicated; otherwise, the word "atha" would have been employed only at the beginning of the verses. By the word "dīkṣā," the visual initiation (*cākṣuṣa*) and others to be described later are meant, as well as the *pratiṣṭhā*.

By the word *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), the rites of installation (*sthāpanā*) and so forth, which will be described, are meant. The meaning is that there are two seeds for both [the Buddha and the stūpa]: the cause of *nirvāṇa* and the cause of *pratiṣṭhā*.
Alternatively, it is the state of being the motivator for activity in both cases that is subsumed therein.
Because [the teachings] are very extensive in the Āgamas, they are being summarized for the sake of easy comprehension;
"by us" is the ellipsis of the sentence. By this, it is stated that one's own words are not to be disregarded because they are rooted in authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*). In this regard:

Regarding these two seeds of nirvāṇa, some say as follows: when consciousness is isolated (*vijñānakaivalya*), there is one nirvāṇa characterized by the cessation of the *prakṛti’s* functional authority (*adhikāra*), which is synonymous with the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā*. This is because, for those who have transcended karma, only the *mala* (impurity) remains.
Furthermore, in the other case, there is the direct manifestation of Śiva-nature preceded by the power of authority and liberation.
In the latter case, however, initiation alone constitutes one form of Nirvāṇa, just as it does for one who has been initiated [into the Vedic order].
Just as a young brahmin, even though his body remains as it was before, acquires a second name through the rite called initiation by the power of the scriptures; so too [is it here].

Likewise here too, liberation is the state of being a living soul characterized by *nirvāṇa* through initiation (*dīkṣā*); however, for others, it is the manifestation of the nature of Śiva following the fall of the body.
Others, however, [say]:
The threefold and twofold nature [of the womb], the sequence, and the twofold nature of Nirvāṇa. (p.
803) Indeed, the womb of a person is twofold: that consisting of the mother, and that consisting of the universal dissolution of the self.

"He stands alone in every womb"—therefore, there is the Nirvāṇa called "the final birth" (*apaścimajanma*), for after that there is no further birth for him. Although it is the womb that is the material cause of the universe, it is also the manifestation of Śiva-nature; thus, due to its dual nature as both transcendent and immanent, Nirvāṇa is twofold.
In all three of these positions, because there is no cessation of experience (*bhukti*), there is no such thing as liberation (*nirvāṇa*);
for the contradiction characterized by the non-coexistence of enjoyment and liberation is difficult to avoid.
Now, following the order of the enumeration, first [the author] intends to explain the initiation of the *dhenu*.
He describes initiation (*dīkṣā*) and its cause,
as well as how the state of Śiva is manifested through the disjunction from the three bonds:
that initiation is said to be characterized by devotion and detachment.

Just as by the threefold method, there is the dissociation from the three bonds— the three bonds consisting of impurity (mala), māyā, and karma which will be described hereafter— along with the cessation of that bondage; so too, the state of Śiva, which already exists within the self but is concealed by impurities, is [revealed] as omniscience like that of Śiva.
The form consisting of agency and so forth is manifested; that manifestation, moreover, is what kind?
It is devotion characterized by dispassion toward Śiva. That devotion is eightfold or ninefold.
As it is stated by the Lord in the *Śivadharmottara*:
One should feel joy at the birth of my devotees, as well as at their worship; one should personally perform worship and engage in physical activities for my sake.
Devotion to hearing my stories, physical transformations such as tears and horripilation, constant mindfulness of me, and living by subsisting upon what is offered to me.
This eightfold devotion indeed exists within me, like ashes on the body; he is the illustrious sage Aṣṭāvakra, the son of Śyāparṇa, and he is truly wise.

Ninefold devotion has been declared as follows: hearing [the name] of Śambhu, chanting it, remembering Him, washing His feet, worshipping Him, applying sandalwood paste, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender. Thus has ninefold devotion been proclaimed by the Lord Śambhu.
Dispassion toward *saṃsāra* arises from a sense of revulsion regarding the experience of infinite births and deaths, as well as pleasure and pain; thus, it is to be abandoned.
Both of these characteristics define [the nature of] that which is not to be characterized.
The definition is "that which makes known" or "that which sets in motion"; the meaning is "that which initiates the primary cause.

By this, it is established that only those possessing devotion (*bhakti*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) have the qualification for initiation (*dīkṣā*). And the root of those two is precisely the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*), and the cause of that is the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*). As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmṛgendra*,
it is said that for those embodied beings upon whom grace descends so as not to turn back,
their indicative signs are a longing for liberation and an aversion to worldly existence.
Likewise, according to the Vāmadeva [Tantra],
the preceptor is worthy of bestowing grace upon the disciple in accordance with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); where power has not descended,
there purity does not arise.
p.

805) There is no knowledge, no auspicious conduct, no liberation, nor the nine supernatural powers; therefore, having observed the signs of an abundant descent of power (śaktipāta), [one acts] either through knowledge or through ritual action.
The teacher should purify the disciple.
Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The time for the descent of that [grace] is equalized with the [remaining] karma; the equality of karmas refers to whether the time is exhausted or equal."
However, when there is a relationship of deficiency or excess in karma, confusion indeed arises regarding the objects of experience.
The absence of that [confusion] is the attainment of power (śakti), which occurs solely through the force of time. This too has been stated in that very same [text].
From the connection of the excessive with the deficient, indeed, confusion arises;
through the deficiency of the excessive, the self attains clarity.

Due to the connection with beginningless seeds, Śiva depends upon time; it is said that time is manifold, and the Lord Śiva is the knower of that. Just as one [aims] at a moving target, something requires a certain amount of time.

The connection is as follows: "If that Śiva, though possessing knowledge, requires [the disciple] at the same time, then this is called the initiation by action (kriyādīkṣā). Thus, the meaning is that it is called *dīkṣā* because it bestows the enjoyment of the soul's nature as Śiva and because it exhausts the connection with the bonds (*pāśa*).
As it has been said:
"The true essence of knowledge is bestowed, and the accumulation of fetters is destroyed.
Because its nature consists of giving and exhausting [impurities], the word *dīkṣā* is used here in this sense.
And thus, since this [initiation] involves the bestowing of these two fruits through a different ritual action, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
The two fruits of that [initiation] proceed precisely according to the degree of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*).
There is also no over-extension [of the definition]. Thus, having stated the definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*),
he states the definition of that initiated person who has transcended the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*), in order to explain the characteristics of the bound soul which impel that initiation.

Therefore, knowledge, devotion, and detachment are the marks of the self that has been initiated here; these do not belong directly to the bound soul (paśu). Since initiation is characterized by devotion and detachment, therefore knowledge is the state of Śiva, which is declared to be the highest of all.

The knowledge that one is the liberator of the fettered souls (*paśu-pāśa-vimocaka*), as well as devotion toward Śiva and detachment from worldly existence— these three are the signs and characteristics of the initiated soul in this very life.
As it has been said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:

"Through knowledge, discernment arises regarding things to be known, those to be abandoned, and those to be adopted; having become detached from both [types of] worldly existence, that which is to be adopted is sought."
Having recognized that the auspicious [Śiva] is what is to be accepted, one then practices devotion to Him;
thereafter, one intensely seeks out a Guru who is a promoter of the path of devotion.
"In the Pauṣkara [Tantra] it is said: 'The bound soul (paśu), initiated by a gracious Guru through the internal initiation, becomes liberated from saṃsāra.'"
Dispassion toward this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra arises quickly; O Lord of Gods, when shall I behold liberation from bondage? When shall I be liberated?
"Who is the one who reveals [the truth], O Śambhu?"—such a thought arises;
in this way, the Lord bestows grace upon those who are distressed by saṃsāra.

Now, one might object: "Could it not be that devotion, knowledge, and dispassion arise even for one who is uninitiated, by virtue of meritorious deeds performed in previous lives? To this, he says: "Of the bound soul (paśoḥ)"—for the uninitiated bound soul, these qualities such as devotion and the rest are not truly real in their direct sense.

Although these may occasionally arise by the power of merit from previous births, they are nevertheless as fleeting as the light of a firefly; however, for one who has been initiated, [these powers] arise through the grace of the Guru, who is Śiva himself.
The meaning is that, by the power of her sidelong glances, they become like adamantine spikes (*vajrakīla*). According to Amara, *satye tv ardha-añjasā vayam* [is used];

however, when it is said that for the bound soul (*paśu*) these are not straightforward (*na añjasā*), then initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself is characterized as both the fetter (*pāśa*) and the one who binds (*pāśaka*).

In order to make known the cause, he states the definition of the bound soul (paśu): "The bound soul is one who possesses limited knowledge, is subject to dissolution, is distinct [from the Lord], and is the agent and enjoyer of its own actions."

The soul is endowed with a body, all-pervading, eternal, susceptible to refinement, possessed of a Lord, and a bound creature (paśu). It is called "limited knowledge" (kiñcijjña) because it knows only a little; however, unlike the liberated soul (muktātman), it does not possess omniscience.
Therefore, limited knowledge alone is the defining characteristic of the bound soul (paśu). For by this much alone,
[the bound soul] is distinguished from both the Lord (pati) and the fetter (pāśa), since the Lord possesses omniscience while the fetter is devoid of knowledge.

Thus, they say that for the others, however, there is merely the status of being a qualifying attribute that indicates something. For this very reason, they say: "malina" means bound by primordial impurity (*anādimala*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Because it is connected with beginningless impurity, Śiva is said to possess the impurity of the atom; because he is liberated from beginningless impurity, he abides as the stainless Śiva."
Therefore, he is distinct, being excluded from the Lord;
the sense is that the individual soul (jīva) is not the Lord himself. They state the reason for his impurity:
because, through his own actions—both merit and demerit—he is both the agent and the experiencer, yet remains dependent on another.
This is the state of being. Regarding enjoyment (*bhoga*), however, the word "karma" refers to pleasure, pain, and so forth;
by its own term, it denotes the state of having fixed objects.
It is said to be "of enjoyments," and regarding enjoyment, he states the means: "possessing a body and the like."

[The soul] is enriched and endowed with bodies corresponding to their respective merits and demerits; otherwise, various diverse experiences would be impossible. Now, one might ask: how can that which is endowed with a body, being limited in its perception and eternal, [experience] what occurs in another place or in another birth?

Regarding that, he states [the following] concerning the state of being the enjoyer of the fruits of karma: "Omnipresent and eternal. Here, "omnipresent" (*vibhu*) means pervasive and completely full. "Eternal" (*nitya*) means devoid of non-existence throughout the three periods of time.
[This applies] to the enjoyment that occurs in other locations...

The cause is manifold; thus, the cause for experience occurring in another birth is eternal, otherwise there would arise the fallacy of a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) between the experience and its causes. But [an objection is raised]: nanu...

Since objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*) are infinite, insentient, and because this [individual soul] possesses only limited knowledge and is impure, how can there be a fixed determination of objects among those enjoyments? To this, he says:
"Together with the Lord" (*seśvara*). This means accompanied by the Lord; that is to say, dependent upon the Lord. As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
O bull among the twice-born, since this living being is ignorant and lacks self-control, even he must depend on something else for his own activity, just like a suckling calf.
How can he be accepted as the agent? Therefore, [the status of] Maheśvara [is not established].

This characteristic of the bound soul (*paśu*) has been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Śataratnasaṅgraha*; we do not elaborate upon it here. And thus, because actions are eternal, for him...
To the question, "How can there be the state of being the enjoyer of a fruit that occurs in another place and at another time? he says:
"The object to be refined (saṃskārya) is the refinement (saṃskāra), which is a specific unseen force (adṛṣṭaviśeṣa) produced by name-and-form and karma."

One who is fit for that [initiation] and has indeed undergone the purificatory rites such as *dīkṣā* is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*). And this definition of a bound soul is common to both the *vijñānākala* and the *pralayākala*.
The specific characteristics of the purifier in the form of *kāla* (time) will be explained later.
And so it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The bound soul (*paśu*) is autonomous, consisting of pure consciousness alone, yet defiled by impurities."

p. 810) "He is deluded, wandering in saṃsāra, possessing limited knowledge, lacking sovereignty, and inactive"— having thus stated the characteristics of the bound soul (paśu), [the author now addresses] the threefold bondage beginning with impurity (mala) within initiation (dīkṣā).
To indicate that knowledge (*jñāna*) is also subject to activity because it is something to be purified, [the author] states the definition of the fetters (*pāśa*):
"The fetters are also to be known as three: impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and action (*karman*). Here, regarding impurity (*mala*)...
The group of consciousnesses (*vijñāna-kalā*), the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala* are mentioned first because they constitute the primary fetters (*pāśa*) for all three [categories of souls].
Following that, [the fetter] of Māyā is mentioned, as it is the fetter for both [the remaining two categories] who are distinct from the *vijñānākala*.
Since everything is indeed a bond (*pāśa*), immediately following [the discussion of] *karman*,

it is said: "In this regard, the impurity (*mala*)— which consists of both the stain (*malina*) and the knot (*grantha*)— spontaneously obscures knowledge and action within the self, which is otherwise established by itself."
If it is argued that impurity (*mala*) is beginningless [and thus not a product], [the response is: "of men" (*puṃsām*).

Furthermore, although this [impurity] is included within the category of *pāśa* (bond), it is also included within *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul); for without it, the very state of being a *paśu* would not exist.

For this very reason it has been said: "The bound soul (paśu) is so called because of its conjunction with the state of being a bound soul. Now, one might object: according to the statements of the *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other scriptures, such as "consciousness is the nature of action, and that [consciousness] exists eternally in the Self," the Self possesses the nature of Śiva, characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and consisting of pure consciousness.
Since it is established that [impurity] exists at all times, its correlate—bondage (paśutva)—is also established by virtue of the beginninglessness of that impurity.
If it is asked, "How can Śivatva and Paśutva, which exist in mutual opposition like light and darkness, reside in a single self?"—
this is true; however, the Śivatva of the Self, consisting of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, is established even while [the state of] being food and so on exists.

Because it has been defiled by beginningless impurities, its power to perceive objects remains latent within itself due to being obstructed— just as the gold-ness existing in copper is obscured by its surface luster— and thus it abides only within its own object.

However, it is not the case that the soul's insentience has been produced by him through the destruction of its own essential nature. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, then just like eternity and other such attributes, the soul's state of being a bound animal (paśutva)— being corrupted by the impurity of *āṇava* and other *mala*s— would likewise be irremediable.

Just as copper pierced by mercury manifests its nature as gold, so too is the manifestation of the Śiva-nature of the Self pierced by knowledge logically established. As it has been stated in the Sarvajñānottara: "Just as copper pierced by mercury is transformed into the state of gold."
Likewise, the self, being conjoined with knowledge, is established as Śiva-nature. Here,

"conjoined with knowledge" (jñānasambhinna) means being united with that activity of Śiva in the form of the Guru known as the "lamp-eye" (dīpakṣa), which manifests all-objective knowledge by means of which "everything is known."

For the cessation of the impurity of the self is established through the very activity of the Lord known as *dīkṣā*, just as the removal of a cataract from the eye is achieved through the medical treatment of a physician; or for that very reason, [it is taught] for the sake of liberating the self’s impurity from the bondage of karma known as *māyā*.

And regarding the statement in the *Svāyambhuva* that "knowledge proceeds from Śiva for the manifestation of the state of Śiva-ness," it has been explained by the Teachers that "Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*) proceeds. For this very reason:
In that very context, it has been stated: "Initiation alone liberates; it leads upward to the state of Śiva and does not bind.
Now, one might object: since initiation is an action (*karman*), like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others, it must result only in bondage and cannot be the cause of liberation. This is true.

Just as a physician (*jāṅgalika*) removes poison through the power of mantras and by means of meditative practices (*dhyāna*) and other rites, so too does the Noble One (*ārya*) effect the severance of the bonds (*pāśa*), such as impurity (*mala*), solely through the rite consisting of initiation (*dīkṣā*) consecrated by the names Śiva and Śaṅkara.
It indeed brings about the manifestation of one's own Śiva-nature; as it has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:

"Just as [a mantra] effects the removal of poison through the power of meditation and seed-syllables, so too does the Guru effect the severance of the bonds (pāśa) through the sacrifices of Śiva. Furthermore:
It is heard in scripture that liberation from misdeeds occurs through rites such as expiation.

Thus, here too, there is no contradiction in speaking of "release from the bond" (*pāśamokṣa*). Now, since it is accepted that impurity (*mala*) is beginningless and eternal, its quality of obscuring the Self is self-evident, just as heat is inherent to fire. And so, the destruction of impurity itself is the destruction of its power to obscure.

If it is argued that [the destruction of impurity] is possible, just as the destruction of heat occurs upon the destruction of fire, we reply: no, because since impurity is eternal, its destruction is not possible.
However, the binding power of impurities (*mala*) and other fetters (*pāśa*) is rendered inactive, just as the lethal potency of a poisonous plant is neutralized.
There is no contradiction in [the statement] "by means of initiation.
Now, an objection: if impurity (*mala*) were gross and manifold, it would follow that it is non-eternal, like a jar or similar objects.

And thus, unity alone must be accepted. As it has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "If that were the case, then upon the cessation of that [one soul], there would be the undesirable consequence of the liberation of all. If this is argued:
Even though that impurity (*mala*) is unitary, it is admitted to have a manifold nature because it possesses multiple powers;
thus, for each individual soul (*ātman*), there exists a collection of powers that persists until the end of its own respective time. — *Cintyaviśva*.

For the *bhāṇava* substance is indeed of a single form, yet it possesses various powers; like copper, its blackness is also innate and does not come from elsewhere. Just as the husk is innate to the grain of rice, so too is impurity (*mala*) said to be innate. And thus, by the ripening of a single power of that impurity...
When that [ignorance] ceases, then liberation belongs to that very [self] and not to another; this is established, so enough with prolixity.
Māyā is the cause of the world, and it is a real entity (vastubhūta) and impermanent. Now, as for the Vedāntins—
It is deluded and false in form.
As it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: [p. 814]
And Māyā is the primordial, pure substance of the universe; she is eternal.

Karma consists of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), for it is established by the Veda, since it is accessible only through the singular authority of the Veda. Thus it has been stated in the Svāyambhuva [Tantra]:

"Through the knowledge of the Dharmaśāstra, [one attains] the state of being born of the gods. Having thus indicated the subject matter, he states its definition: "Impurity is impurity, which is ignorance; it is that which obstructs consciousness.
Thus, "impurity" is the very definition of *mala*. To the question of what kind of thing this impurity is, he says:

"Ignorance" (*ajñāna*) means that which is opposed to knowledge (*jñāna*). Among the meanings of the verbal root *jñā*—namely, non-existence, opposition, and being other than that—the negative particle here has the sense of opposition. For this very reason, it is said to be the opponent of the consciousness that has been brought forth; [it is] the nature of the Self, consisting of such qualities as omniscience established by itself.
The meaning is "that which is opposed. He describes the characteristic of *māyā* by way of its effects:
"The collection of principles (*tattvasaṃhṛti*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth; *kalā* is the first, and earth is the last of that collection of principles. *Tattva*...

The aggregate: that which arises from the proximity of Bhava is Māyā; it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Kāla and ending with Earth. This is the meaning of "Māyā.
Now, he states the definition of *karman*: action consists of merit and demerit; this is clear.
To the question of to whom these three bonds belong, he says: "Because by these bonds [there is] the bound soul (paśu).

The meaning is that for some there is the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) through fetters (*pāśa*), for others through impurity (*mala*), for some through both impurity and *māyā*, for some through impurity, *māyā*, and action (*karman*), and for others through the bond [itself]. Thus, it is indicated that the essential definition of being a bound soul is simply the state of being bound by fetters.

This is the function of the three bonds (*pāśatraya*). He demonstrates [this] with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*): due to the ignorance of the bound soul, there is a connection with *māyā* for the sake of the experience of karmas; because the consciousness of the bound soul is veiled by impurity (*mala*), there is a connection with *māyā*. The very connection with the categories (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth is indeed the connection with the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).

The meaning is "thus. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "karmas exist for the sake of experience," that is, for the experience of pleasure and pain. This is established in the *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra] in the determination [of its nature]: "Experience is the sensation of persons, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. Immediately...

The group of principles beginning with the earth is determined for every city by the masters of light (jyotirācāryas), extending down to the level of the *kalā*. And as stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "By the power of karma, this [group] exists within all worlds and bodies."
"From the *payoktra* up to the *mahī*, this [set of implements] accomplishes the purpose of the staff (*daṇḍārtha*).
In the *Pauṣkara*: "The reality (*tattva*) is fixed for each person, beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*avani*). Also, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: [same as above].
Endowed with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka*, [the soul] exists within all wombs by the power of karma;
the *puryaṣṭaka* consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), intellect (*dhī*), and the instruments of action (*karmakaraṇāni*). Now, in the *Śrīkālottara*:
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell constitute the pentad;
along with intellect, mind, and ego—this is always called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) within the heart. Thus it is heard in scripture.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can the categories beginning with *kalā* be of the nature of the principles (*tattva*) down to earth?"—this is true; however, on the occasion of explaining the Sūtra, the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha, in accordance with the *Mṛgendra*, explained it precisely as consisting of thirty principles. That being so...

To the doubt as to how its "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) is not [the self], [the answer is: by means of the five groups known as the elements, time, the intellect, the sense organs, the organs of action, and the internal organ, together with their cause— the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva)— and the Pradhāna which fills them.
And there is no contradiction because [the soul] is enveloped by the triad consisting of the five sheaths beginning with *kalā*, which serve as auxiliaries to its nature as an enjoyer;
thus it has been resolved by Aghoraśivācārya.

But if it is asked how there can be liberation for the self, which is bound by the three bonds beginning with *samaya* and has been so since beginningless time, he says: "Liberation occurs through the will [of the Lord] regarding *samaya* and the rest; it does not happen otherwise. Therefore, due to its own karma, this bound soul (*paśu*) experiences the full range of enjoyments, such as pleasure and the like. Its *samayas* are as follows:

The ritual refinement of the *samaya* (vow) is the beginning of that which is called initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the will of the Lord; from that very [initiation] arises the specific *samaya* known as "nirvāṇa," and liberation is indeed the state of initiation itself.
It follows that there is release from the three bonds—this is the remainder [of the sense]. Otherwise, it would be established by other scriptures.
From another perspective, for this reason—that is, from whatever cause—there is no such statement as "one becomes [liberated]";
[this refers to] the notions of liberation established in other treatises.
Because it consists in the attainment of various lower levels of reality (*tattva*) than Śiva-nature, because it is characterized by gradation,

and because it involves returning once more, it does not constitute liberation due to the absence of release from the bondage of the three fetters (*pāśa*). This [state], however, is indeed liberation, because it consists in the attainment of the state of Śiva as described above.
Because it is free from rebirth and because it effects liberation from the bondage of the three fetters, it possesses reality according to its true nature.
As it has been said:
"The Carvakas, those who know the Kālika-jyotiḥ-śāstra, and the Bhautikas [are absorbed] into the Tanmātras."

The Siddhas and Smārtas maintain that the eye and other senses are the Supreme; the Vaiśeṣikas, however, hold them to reside in the quality of *saṃskāra*. The Buddhists are established in the principle of consciousness (*buddhi-tattva*), while the Jains are established in the qualities (*guṇa*). Those who know the Pañcarātra consider *prakṛti* to be Hari.
The knowers of Vedānta and the Sāṃkhyas abide in the Puruṣa;
the Pāśupatas abide in Māyā, while those of the Great Vow abide in Vidyā.
In the Śakti-tattva, those who are non-dual with it are situated in the supreme Śiva-tattva; as stated in the Mṛgendra,
that which is liberation arises from the discrimination between the individual soul (puṃs) and primordial nature (prakṛti), or else by considering everything as Brahman.

Pause. Whatever liberations arise from bondage, they all attain non-difference within the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). In the Śaiva system, the perfected ones (*siddha*) reach the summit; among them, in the liberation of emanation, the one who is superior to the individual soul (*puruṣa*) is not below [the others].
"Having supported all things by His own power, the Lord of All remains forever as the sovereign ruler.

Therefore, according to another scripture, because there is no liberation [from karma], one experiences the entirety of enjoyment—consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth—solely through one's own actions, namely by means of the merits and demerits one has performed oneself; thus, "enjoyment" (bhoga) refers to the fact that one enjoys that [experience]. Now, release the fruit.
He states the result:

"The transmigrating soul, along with the animal [of karma], is bound; it is liberated when endowed with the three-fold bond. Due to the power of the bondage of the three-fold bond, the transmigrating soul undergoes many births, deaths, pleasures, and pains."

The bound soul (paśu) is bound; it is said to be bound because of the bondage of the three fetters (pāśa). It is possessed of the three fetters. Released from the three fetters through initiation (dīkṣā), it is said to be liberated.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*, it is said by the wise: "One who perceives the self as enveloped by impurities is called 'impure';
one who perceives the self as freed from impurities is called 'pure'. Now, [one might object]:

It is said that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the liberation from the three bonds (*pāśatraya*). Regarding this, there may be the doubt as to whether all souls (*ātman*) are bound by the three bonds from the very beginning, or whether some are bound by some [bond] or another; therefore, in order to distinguish those [cases], he states the classification of bound souls (*paśubheda*).

This [bound soul] to be favored is threefold: the sakala (with parts), the pralayākala (inactive due to dissolution), and the vijñānākala (devoid of mental constructs). Now their essential nature is described. "To be favored" means the object of Śiva’s grace in the form of initiation; this refers to the previously mentioned bound soul (baddha-paśu), which is of three kinds.
"Of three kinds"— the singular is used for the class (*jātāv ekavacanam*).
He states those very types:

*Sakala* is one who is bound by *kalā* along with [the other *tattvas*]. *Pralayākala* is one who, at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), is devoid of being bound by *kalā*. *Vijñānākala* is one who, through direct *vijñāna*—that is, the power of the Lord’s knowledge—is devoid of being bound by *kalā*. Thus it is.

Their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is threefold; for if it were not fully known, engagement in initiation would simply not be possible—thus one recognizes its status as a characteristic. Their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is also their characteristic. This is now stated: this is also knowledge (*jñāna*).
The sense is that even the knowledge of the distinctions in the scope of authority regarding the different types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is, in this context, the seed of initiation.
He states the definition according to the order of enumeration.

The *sakala* [individual], covered by the impurities of *māyā*, *karman*, and *mala*, is also dissolved; likewise, those who are enveloped by the impurities of *mala* and *karman* become *pralayākalas*.

One bound by impurity alone is called *vijñānākala*. Likewise, in the universe of the conceivable (*cintyaviśva*), one joined with impurity is the first; one joined with both impurity and karma is the second; and one joined with the impurities of *mala*, *māyā*, and *karma* is called *sakala*. These [states] proceed from the beginningless impurity and *māyā*, which have been flowing since time without beginning.
And when karma is present, he is called "sakala" (with parts); he is called "kalā-yukta" (endowed with a portion).
Due to the partial removal of impurity from the innate knowledge and agency of the Puruṣa, he is known as "kalāmālin" (garlanded with portions).

She manifests the totality of the *kalās*. Thus it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*: "In this manner, she again produced the *kalās* in due order, having pierced through the *āṇava-mala* without deficiency, all at once."

Having established the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*) within the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), one should manifest it; for the purpose of binding the *kalās*, this reality of *kalā* is proclaimed for the sake of the enjoyment of the ignorant, and not for the sake of liberation. [Objection: But since the Self possesses the quality of being a knower...

The power that manifests agency is called *kalā*. If it is argued, "Let that [agency] arise through the very power of Śiva; what is the need for *kalā*?", we reply: Śiva does not manifest the soul's capacity for knowledge and agency without the fetter (*pāśa*). It is just as wind, bile, and other humors do not produce disease without unwholesome food.
And he causes affliction; as it has been stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*:

"But [Śiva] manifests the noose in the Lord of the Net (Vitāneśa); just as that fault is not uneven regarding all objects, so too, 'Śiva is the agent of disease for us who are on the side of the wicked,' [is said]. Now, [one might object]:...
Kalā is accepted for the sake of manifesting the soul's own capacity for experience and agency;
let that [manifestation] arise through karma alone, which is the cause of experience, and not in the absence of it, through consciousness.
If it is argued that this is because there is an absence of experience [of the fruits] of the *kalās*, [we reply:
since the various *karmas* are exhausted merely by producing their respective experiences, and because there is no evidence for their being causes of any other effect;
furthermore, since a *karman* only becomes the cause of experience when assisted by another *tattva*, [in the absence of such assistance], the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth [would not function].
Even the principles (*tattvas*) would then be devoid of purpose. [Objection:
But in that case, it follows that the knowledge and vision of the Self, which were previously non-existent, arise only through the conjunction with *kalā*.

Knowledge arises through the conjunction with its constituent parts (*kalā-yoga*). Just as the cognition of a jar arises from the contact of the sense organs [with the object], so too the Self possesses the very nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), and not the nature of being knowledge itself (*jñānarūpatva*). If it were argued that [the Self] is indeed of the nature of knowledge, [we reply]:
no; for the absence of the Self's status as a knower is not due to its non-existence, but rather [due to its being unmanifest]. However—
Just as there is no cognition of a jar enveloped in darkness solely due to the absence of a manifestor—
such as a lamp— and not because of its non-existence; so too,
if one accepts that [consciousness] is eternal knowledge, it would follow that it is non-eternal due to its association with modification.

Furthermore, since the nature of the self as a knower is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) precisely when the manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) is present, one must admit that the self's nature as consciousness is indeed eternal; yet,
because it was previously veiled by beginningless impurities, it did not [manifest] due to the lack of connection with the manifesting *kalā*.

It manifests; since it is precisely through its conjunction with that [kalā] that it manifests, the connection with *kalā* must be accepted based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). It is precisely through this conjunction that the Self possesses the state of being *sakala* (endowed with parts); enough of this elaboration. And this constitutes the connection with the three bonds (*pāśatraya*), being enveloped by impurity (*mala*) and karma.

That which is enveloped by primordial impurity (*mala*) and by *karman* is called *pralaya-kalā*, because through *pralaya* there is the withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *kalās* and other [principles]. It is called *bandha* (bondage) because one is bound by a connection tied solely to *mala*. It is a *pāśa* (fetter).
He who possesses a connection with only the single bond called *mala* is called a *vijñānākala*.
[This occurs] through the practice of knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, renunciation (*sannyāsa*), or from the exhaustion of karma through experience.

"Kṣaya" (destruction) means that through this consciousness, there is an absence of both karma—intended for its enjoyment—and the bondage of the *kalās* and so forth; thus, here the term "sakala" refers to the *sakalas*, *pralayākalas*, and *vijñānakalas*, where "sakala" is used in the singular to denote the class (*jāti*). And those *sakalas* [are so called] because their impurity (*mala*) is fully ripened.

They are of two kinds: those whose impurities are fully ripened and those whose impurities are not. Among them, those whose impurities are fully ripened proceed toward liberation through initiation performed by a teacher who is Śiva in form. As it has been said:
"He unites these [disciples] whose impurities are fully ripened with the Supreme Reality by means of the descent of power (śaktipāta), which is the cause of their eradication."
"By initiation, [the soul] resides in the form of the Teacher (ācārya-mūrti-stha)," so it is said. Others, however, are worldly beings (saṃsārin).
These include the *pralayākalas*, who are further divided into those whose impurities (*mala*) and karma are fully ripened and those whose impurities and karma are not yet ripened.
Among them, for those whose impurities and karma are fully ripened, Śiva grants liberation through initiation alone, without requiring further ritual substrates (*niradhikaraṇa-dīkṣā*).
It causes [the soul] to attain [that state]. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Upon the cessation of the authority of darkness (tamas) and its subsequent withdrawal, Śiva, the kinsman of the world, manifests for the individual soul (aṇu) his non-differentiated vision and action."
When that [world] of Svāyambhuva has perished, she (Prakṛti) leads him to the supreme liberation. Others, however,
being restrained by the body of the eightfold city, become embodied yogins who attain the status of lords of the worlds.

Yet among them, some— by means of the Lord Ananta’s grace according to the gradations of their maturation— attain the status of lords of the five groups of eight worlds known as Guhya, Atiguha, Guhyātiga, Pavitra, Sthānu, and Āpya;
having reached the end of their respective offices, they become endowed with manifest knowledge, action, the power of atomization (aṇimā), and the other [siddhis].

As it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "Having selected certain [souls] to be graced, Maheśvara bestows upon them the status of world-lords (*bhuvanapati*) as well as the powers of knowledge and action. (p. 823)

It is twofold, by way of the distinction between mature impurity (*pakvamala*) and immature impurity (*apakvamala*). Among these, those who possess the status of an *avidyeśa* have mature impurity, while others are the seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantra*).
Even in that case, there occurs the removal of half the [remaining] bonds and the bestowal of Śiva’s grace. Therefore:

The half [of the path] is the instrument for the grace of Śiva, which pertains to the substratum. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "In the entire path, that [grace], depending on the body of the agent, exercises its authority over the tasks."

At the end of the period of maintenance, he enters Śiva, the Lord; without a further substratum, there is no other manifestation or transformation. Having relinquished the authority over his functions within the Lords, he is withdrawn into his own self. Thus it is said: And likewise:
By the power of this mantra alone, the desired enjoyment of worlds and liberation come to practitioners.
As it is said in the venerable *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*:
"Wherever one may desire enjoyments, there indeed is one joined [to them]."
Through the power of the perfected mantra, and likewise through the practice of what has been taught, [one attains this]. And in the *Śrīmad-Ārāva*:

"Purified by initiation, born within the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru, those who have attained perfection through mantras possess bodies radiant with the splendor of the rising orb of the young sun; having enjoyed..."

"Endowed with enjoyments accompanied by hosts of celestial women who take great delight, and having their longing aroused, they become partakers of the sovereignty of the supreme state of Śiva. Now, it is said that for the *sakala* [souls], the cessation of bondage arises through initiation (*dīkṣā*). If it is asked, "How can this be known?"—
It is said: as stated in the *Śrīmat Kālottara* and other texts (p.
824), having examined the dignity of that self by means of the imposition of the state of being consecrated by the mantra;

Just as one who has been bitten by a snake is seen to experience a throbbing sensation when the snake is placed back upon him after first performing the recitation of the mantra for the backward step (*paścādṛkpāda*), so too do those bitten by poison say that [the effect] occurs both before and after the actions of the snake-charmer (*āhituṇḍika*).

And likewise, in the *Satvasaṅgraha*: "One should know that when one is weighed on a scale after initiation (*dīkṣā*), the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) has departed from them; it is like the removal of bonds or the destruction of poison. Now, [one might ask: if all fetters (*pāśa*) are destroyed by initiation, [how can this be so?]

If it is argued that there would be the consequence of the body falling [into ashes] at that very moment, that is true. Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of two kinds: that which leads to liberation after death (*asadyonirvāṇā*) and that which leads to liberation in this life (*sadyonirvāṇā*). Among these, in the case of initiation leading to liberation after death, [it functions] by burning away only those karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in future births.

The maintenance of *prārabdha* karmas is solely for the purpose of experiencing their fruits. As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "The *karman* pertaining to many births has been burnt by the individual souls like a seed;
even that which is yet to come is restrained by Him through experience—this indeed is immediate liberation."

Indeed, through initiation (*dīkṣā*), even karma that has already begun to bear fruit (*prārabdhakarman*) is certainly destroyed; nevertheless, the mere maintenance of the body may still occur for some time. As it is said by Garuḍa in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "O Lord, if all the bonds of the universe are entirely destroyed by Your initiation..."

Once the purpose has been accomplished upon birth, how could the persistence of the body remain? Just as the wheel continues to spin even after the pot has been completed by the Blessed Potter, so too does this body persist, sustained by the momentum of prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*).
He remains [in the body], sustained by the force of his residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) like the whirling of a potter’s wheel. But surely,
since he attains Nirvāṇa immediately, there will be no future birth following initiation (*dīkṣā*).

When the body remains for a period beyond that stated for initiation (*dīkṣā*), even though previously commenced actions persist for the sake of experiencing their fruits, what is the destiny of the actions performed during that time? [What is the result] of action performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*)?

Because the result is necessarily bound to occur; that is, in the case of failing to perform [prescribed duties] and performing prohibited actions. One should not transgress the conduct of one's caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) with the mind. Furthermore, in whichever stage of life one may abide, having received initiation whose essence is Śiva—

If it is argued that there are scriptural injunctions such as, "One should remain established in that very state and protect the duties of a living being," and that by transgressing this command one is said to become a flesh-eater for a hundred years, and so forth—thereby establishing that there is a sin (pratyavāya) in failing to perform [the duty]—it is replied: [The response follows: It is said:
Rites performed after the time specified for initiation do not bring about results that manifest in another birth; rather, they remain [without effect] according to the maxim of the burnt cloth.
As it is said in the *Tattvanirṇaya*: "Even if [the rite] is performed by one who has been initiated..."
Like a seed at the edge of a pond. Thus, there is a certain period following the initiation (*dīkṣā*) as described.
Having performed the conduct of the *samaya* and being like a *piśāca*, one experiences sovereignty; immediately thereafter comes liberation.
As it is said in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*: "Therefore, one who has not performed the ritual... [and so forth]. A little.
Even for those who have died at the appointed time, by the fault of transgressing his command, one becomes for some time a king of the foremost Piśācas;
then, having wandered about with a purified soul, he indeed attains equality with the Supreme Lord. Thus it is said.
And thus, there is not even a single hair’s breadth of doubt regarding both the seeded initiation (*sabīja-dīkṣā*) and the seedless initiation (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*); enough of this digression. Thus...
Having addressed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiations— divided into the categories of *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala*—

and having stated that liberation consists in the various types of initiation according to the degree of the descent of their respective powers (*śakti-nipāta*), he now declares the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā-bīja*) in its twofold nature: as being without support (*nirādhāra*) and with support (*sādhāra*).

The grace (*anugraha*) of Śiva is twofold: it is the desire of Śiva to liberate the bound soul (*paśu*) from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and that [desire] is the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*). It is twofold by way of being with support (*sādhāra*) and without support (*nirādhāra*). Among these, that which proceeds without the intervention of the *māyā* of the form of a teacher (*ācārya*) is the supportless (*nirādhāra*).

He who, having presided over the form of the Ācārya, is the common support for all; likewise, she who is the support of the entire universe of thought yet is herself without support—she is the support of everyone, while others are called "without support. Thus has initiation been declared by me. This very [point].

I have also [discussed] this through the distinction of causes and the distinction of objects. Śiva, having looked upon the teacher, bestows grace in two ways due to the descent of his power (*śakti-nipāta*). He himself favors those who have realized the categories of dissolution (*pralaya-kalā*). "He desires" means "he shines"; the meaning is that he is self-luminous by nature.

The word *siṃha* is correct because it is established through the transposition of the letters *vaśa* and *kānti*. As it has been stated by the learned: "The word *siṃha* is derived from the root *hiṃs* [in the sense of harming], while *śiva* is traditionally remembered as being derived from *vaśa* and *kānti*; it is established through the transposition of phonemes. Thus says Kaśyapa.

"Paśyakaḥ yathā" (As the observer): disregarding the teacher, having merely assumed the appearance of the teacher's form, [he perceives] the Vijñāna-pralayākalas and the Vijñānākalas; and if the Pralayākalas are twofold, [they are as follows]. (p.

"Due to the descent of power (śaktinipātanāt)": because of the descent of power, which is twofold according to the distinction between intense and more intense. Among these, the descent of intense power occurs in the Vijñānākala beings; it is even more intense in the Pralayākala beings. For this very reason, the state of being a Vijñānākala belongs to the Pralayākalas.

"Having attained liberation by yourselves after this much time, you who have become weary from the duties assigned by me, you shall now be liberated"— thus [the Lord] seems to take pity on you, bestowing grace upon you by removing the bonds of impurity.

He bestows grace known as *viśeṣānugraha*. As it has been said in the *Cintya*: "O Ācārya, by means of His intense power, Śambhu acts independently toward those called *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*; that activity which occurs within the sphere of action (*kriyākale*) is indeed called *niradhārā*."
Thus it has been proclaimed. Having thus described grace that is without a support (nirādhāra), he speaks of that which has a support (sādhāra):

"Assuming the form of the Teacher (ācārya), the Lord bestows grace upon all beings through the fourth descent of power (śaktipāta). The Lord is endowed with sovereignty and other attributes that are fully manifest."

According to the scriptural statement: "The tradition holds that *bhaga* consists of the sixfold [perfections]: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, as well as knowledge and dispassion," [the Lord] brings down even all those who are bound by the three fetters known as impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and *māyā*, by means of the fourth power (*śakti*).

Through his fourfold innate descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—intense-intense, mild-mild, intense-mild, and mild-intense—he bestows grace (*anugraha*). As it is said in the *Cintyaviśva*, citing the Guru:
"Grace is established through the distinctions of mild, intense, and so forth."
"Out of devotion, Śambhu performs that initiation which is [bestowed] upon one who possesses the requisite qualification;
thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: 'And that which Śambhu performs by virtue of his sovereignty as the fourth [initiation]...'"

"By initiation through the descent of power (śaktipāta), one brings about the end of suffering for all. Now, it may be asked: "Is it not said that initiation occurs according to the degrees of the descent of power? Since power is all-pervasive (vibhu), the very occurrence of its 'descent' is impossible; how, then, can there be degrees? To this, it is replied:
The favor of Śakti is indeed her very presence, yet it is metaphorically designated as a "descent" (nipāta). As it is said in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:
"In this context, the application of words is seen to occur through metaphorical usage (upacāra), just as..."

The omnipresent, eternal, and unchanging Person is said to be perishable when the bonds are severed, just as the King of Mantras is said to be Śiva; likewise, the descent of power (śaktinipāta) is said in the Śiva-āgama to be figurative. Just as the sudden falling of an object occurs out of fear, so too is the descent of power.

Even the Nipāta (the "falling down") is said to bestow the fear of worldly existence. Just as a teacher would awaken sleeping disciples standing before him by means of fire, so too Śiva awakens one who is asleep in the slumber of delusion by means of His Power (Śakti). When there is the realization of one's own true nature, that state is called "fallen" (patita).

I shall describe the characteristics of that [state] and its stages in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, according to the gradations of embodied beings: the falling of the body, as well as trembling, supreme bliss, and exhilaration.

Perspiration and horripilation—this is the characteristic sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, it is said: "The activity of these embodied beings falls [upon them] for the sake of cessation;
their longing for liberation is its mark, as is aversion toward worldly existence and devotion."

Faith in the devotees of Śiva and in the path of His teaching leads even those of dull intellect to the conviction that initiation belongs to Śiva alone, based on the reason of the "learned" (śiṣṭa). Thus, through the section concerning the form of the Teacher, it is established that Śiva alone is the initiator, while others are merely the destroyers of all bonds.

Because of the absence of capacity. Thus, when the seed of initiation known as Śiva’s grace exists, he says that activity arises therein: "Through Śiva’s grace, initiation is born for those who have performed ritual acts—that is, for those whose impurities have been ripened."

O Lord, initiation arises through the grace of Śiva and the descent of power (*śakti-nipāta*); the implication is that others have no authority in this matter. For this very reason, it is taught in scripture that in the absence of the descent of power, both the candidate for initiation (*dīkṣya*) and the initiator (*dīkṣaka*) incur sin. As it is said concerning Vāmadeva:

Where the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has not occurred, there purity does not arise; there is neither knowledge, nor Śiva, nor conduct, nor liberation, nor the supernatural attainments (*siddhis*). Therefore, having repeatedly observed the signs of the descent of power, [one should distinguish] the teacher and the disciple by means of either knowledge or ritual action.
One should purify [the self]. Otherwise, the foolish-minded person who acts out of delusion perishes.

Now, it is stated that the varieties of initiation (*dīkṣā*) arise precisely from the specific ripening of impurities (*malaparipāka*). He sets forth the proposition to describe these varieties of initiation: "And that [initiation] should be known as being of many kinds."

This is called "proliferation" (prapañca). The meaning is that initiation (dīkṣā) has a substratum, whereas obeisance (natir) does not have a substratum, because [obeisance] is accessible solely through Śiva.
He states those very various types that will be described immediately below:

"The visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī*), the tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*), the vocal initiation (*vācikī*), likewise the *mātasī*, the scriptural initiation (*śāstrī*), the yoga initiation (*yogadīkṣā*), the *hautrī*, and so forth—there are many such types. Among these, that which is performed by means of the eye...

The visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī*) consists of the mere sight [of the deity]. The tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*) is accomplished by the laying on of Śiva’s hand, or by the mere utterance of the mantra, or by [the attainment of] liberation.
The mental initiation (*mānasī*) is to be performed through the operations of the mind. [The verbal initiation is] through the study of Śiva’s scriptures...
The *śāstrī* [initiation] is that which is to be set in motion; the *yogadīkṣā* is that which is accessible through the instruction of yoga.

The *bhautrī* [initiation] is preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the offering of water for the feet (*pādodaka-pradāna*), the impulse toward the *akṣi* [eyes], the *bodhaka*, and so on, are indicated. This is according to the order of enumeration.

He states the definition: "Having opened his eyes and meditated, he gazes at the disciple; for the sake of liberating him from the bonds of the fetters, this is considered the ocular initiation (*cākṣuṣī-dīkṣā*). Having meditated on the reality as the form of Śiva—for others, that reality is [designated] by way of metaphor."
This is the state of being. Therefore, meditation on the nature of Śiva is the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Having opened the eyes for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the fetters (*pāśa*), the disciple is gazed upon for the sake of releasing the threefold fetters, such as impurity (*mala*) and the rest; he is beheld through the perfect contemplation of the identity of the self with Śiva.

Thus: the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of "when this occurs. Because the injunction regarding this much initiation (*iyad-īkṣā-vidhi*) is primary, there is a feminine gender designation. It is considered that here [the eyes] are opened and desired; by this statement, the closing [of the eyes] at the time of the recitation is understood.
And so it has been said in the *Vṛddhajñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having closed the eyes and meditated upon that supreme, utterly pure reality, one should then behold..."
This initiation by sight is considered to be for the purpose of purification; here, the word "twofold" refers to enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
Now follows the initiation by touch.
Having placed Śiva, conjoined with the Brahma-aṅgas, in his right hand, he should touch the disciple from the head downwards; this shall be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).

Here too, as there, the phrase "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*) is understood to carry over. Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) proceeds from that [meditation], one should perform it with the five Brahmans and the six limbs joined together.
Śiva is that which conveys the state of Śiva, being the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) due to the non-difference between the signified and the signifier. In the right [hand]...
"In the hand"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "of the preceptor's own. Having placed [it] upon the fingers, he should touch the head and other parts of the disciple;
that is, he should touch the disciple from the head down to the feet. This...

The initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā) occurs as follows. It has been stated therein: "Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva along with the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (aṅgas) in his own hand, the Guru should touch the body of the disciple—its head, back, and so forth. Thus, for one who knows the methods of absorption (laya) and enjoyment (bhoga), there is indeed the initiation by touch."
"Thus it is said: 'Whatever else he touches with his hand, whatever he beholds with his eye—all that becomes auspicious (*śiva*), struck by the rays of the moon of Śiva.
Alternatively, he says to the Vācakī:
"Having concentrated the mind on reality, with the inner luster increased, let her utter the mantras in their continuous sequence; let this initiation proceed."

Having fixed the mind upon the supreme Śiva in reality—that is, having established it there with unwavering steadiness—one becomes one whose inner radiance is expanded; the meaning is that one is filled by the splendor of Śiva residing in the heart-lotus and is thus awakened to the state of identity with the Self of Śiva. This refers to the teacher (ācārya).
The remainder [is as follows]: the *saṃhitā-mantras* of the root *brahmāṅgas*; that which was stated regarding the feminine gender [applies here].
It is said that the *saṃhitā* of the root *brahmāṅgas* is the seat (*sāsana*) of Śiva.

The teacher should cause the disciple to utter [the mantra] by means of cutting his feet; he himself should also utter it. In this way, let initiation proceed; let it proceed in accordance with the disciple's qualification.
The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having established the mind in reality and illuminated by the splendor of the Lord, one whose heart is composed through the initiation of mantra should recite the mantras."
"One should utter the mantras with speech; that is known as the vocal initiation (vācikī-dīkṣā). Now he speaks of the mental [initiation]:
"By resorting to the mental procedure, it is called the mental [initiation]; not by external action."

If every ritual procedure, such as the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala, which is to be performed by one who considers himself a practitioner, is carried out by the mind alone, it is designated as "mental" (mānasī). Thus, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Relying upon the mental procedure, this [initiation] is the mental descent of knowledge (*jñānavamī*)."
833) Now he speaks of the scriptural [initiation]:
"The initiation into the scripture (śāstradīkṣā) is proclaimed by means of the transmission of the scripture. Of the scripture...

The instruction on the Śiva-scriptures, such as the Kāmika and others, as well as the intention for initiation (dīkṣādhiyam), must be undertaken only after the initiation into the rules (samayadīkṣā); otherwise,
one lacks the qualification to hear the Śiva-scriptures.
For this very reason, even the hearing of the Śiva-śāstras constitutes a specific type of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The initiation of the scripture (*śāstradīkṣā*) is declared to be by means of the transmission of the scripture. Now...
Regarding the initiation through yoga (*yogadīkṣā*): by means of yoga, this initiation through yoga is established in his state of Śiva-nature.
Through yoga—namely, through the practice of *dhāraṇā* and so forth, and through the instruction of yoga—this initiation through yoga belongs to this very self.
It is "established" (*vyavasthitā*) in his state of Śiva-nature, meaning it is certain regarding the attainment of the state of Śiva. Having ascertained this...

The sense is that for others, the attainment of the state of Rudra and the attainment of the state of Īśvara constitute the fruit according to their respective capacities (*adhikāra*). For this very reason, the sense is that even this [attainment] must be performed by one who has been consecrated through the *samaya* and other rites. Likewise, it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
In the sense of "going" (yā), the union (yoga) of Śiva and Śivā is called *yajuryoga*; it is clearly stated that their conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is the *yoga* known as the "Shared Path" (*sahamārga*).
The non-existence [of duality] and the state of exhaustion, through knowledge that brings about the existence of reality,
is the union with the principle of Śiva; this is called the initiation of yoga.
Now he speaks of the *hautrī* [line]:

"The *hautrī* is called *rajaṃ-kuṇḍavatī*; it is said to be of two types. Here, the word *rajas* does not refer to the dust-particles corresponding to the colors of Īśāna and the other [deities], but rather denotes the *maṇḍalas* to be accomplished. And so it is said:
Preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala, and consisting of the external and internal rites, it includes specific commitments (*samaya*) and so forth;
this initiation (*dīkṣā*) here is the *hautrī*, which in brief consists of two types of initiation.
And that [initiation] is of two kinds, of two varieties. Now, one might ask: what of this [second type] as well?

Since there is the possibility of many types, such as those based on a single principle (*ekatatva*) and so forth, one might wonder how it is that there are only two divisions. Anticipating this doubt, he says "in brief": "In summary, this initiation is said by the knowers of reality here to be of only two kinds; this initiation pertaining to the *hautra* [officiant] has the *sādhikaraṇa* [the ritual manual] as its basis."

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "by teachers who possess knowledge of its true nature. Here, in this scripture, it is said that there are two kinds, of two types. He states that very twofold nature:
one is known as possessing knowledge (*jñānavatī*), while the other is remembered as possessing ritual action (*kriyāvatī*). One is *jñānavatī*.
It is traditionally held that there may be another [form] which is characterized by activity.

Regarding that, he states the definition of the initiation consisting of knowledge (*jñānavatī-dīkṣā*): "The initiation consisting of knowledge is said to consist solely of mental activity, such as discernment, knowledge, and ritual action;
it arises from the correct realization of reality."

Thus ends [the section on] sacrifice (*yāga*). Since it is stated that "sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity while performing the rites such as *bhoma* which are auxiliary to initiation (*dīkṣā*)," it is not a ritual involving fire (*analakarma*).

The preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*), the preparation of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*), and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the pavilion, the mandala, worship, and other such rites are included—all this [is accomplished] without [physical action], merely through mental activity; that is to say, it is an effect produced solely by mental operation. And that [activity] is perfect.

The initiation consisting of knowledge (*jñānavatī-dīkṣā*) is said to be that which arises from the firm realization of reality and the correct understanding of the purpose of the collection of Śiva’s activities;
otherwise, it would be impossible to accomplish. As it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:

The Guru, who is full and the bestower of the true path, should out of compassion initiate with the initiation of higher knowledge a disciple who has already been prepared by the previously mentioned initiation.

The initiation that exists through mere mental activity is, in sequence, the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*). That which is called "higher knowledge" (*vijñāna*) is indeed bestowed; for Śiva-nature is granted and all doubt is destroyed. Because it possesses such a distinguished form, it is celebrated as "higher knowledge."
Now he states the definition of that which possesses ritual action (*kriyāvatī*):

"That which possesses sacrifice (*ijyā*) and fire (*anala*), and from which skill in ritual action arises, is called 'possessing ritual action' (*kriyāvatī*). Sacrifice is of the nature of a forest (*vana*). Fire is the fire consecrated by the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).

Because both of these [knowledge and action] reside in her, she is "possessing sacrifice and fire" (*ijyānalavatī*). She arises through the capacity for ritual action of the preceptor (*ācārya*), by means of skill in performance such as the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and the pavilion. Initiation that arises from skill in performance is "possessing action" (*kriyāvatī*).

He states the divisions of this very [initiation]: it is manifold; there is the seedless (nibījā) and the seeded (sabījakā), namely, initiation with seeds (bījadīkṣā) and initiation with seeds (sabījadīkṣā).
The phrase "the manifold becomes one" means that the manifold is twofold; thus, [the author] proceeds to define the distinction between the essential natures of both.
First, he states the distinction between the objects [of initiation]:
"In that regard, the seedless [initiation] belongs to the *samayin* and the *putraka*;
however, the seeded initiation belongs to both the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya*."

Here, by the word "seed" (bīja), the practice of the observance (samayācāra) is meant. In that context, those who are beneficial are the "seeded" (bījakā); the "seedless" (nirbījakā) is indeed seedless, meaning independent. She who is thus [seedless] is the "one with the observance" (samayinī), [referring to] the initiate known as a *putraka* who has been consecrated within the tradition called *samaya*.

Even when the subject has been initiated as a *putraka*, it is possible that this teacher desires to make him a *samayin* or a *putraka*; the meaning is that he must perform [the initiation]. He says that this [initiation] is of two kinds: "seedless" (*nibījā*) and "granting immediate liberation" (*sadyo-nirvāṇadā*), which is further divided into two types: that which grants immediate liberation and that which does not grant immediate liberation.
Now, the seedless initiation (nirbījakā dīkṣā) has been described; it is of two kinds.

One bestows nirvāṇa immediately; the second bestows it upon the falling of the body. That which bestows liberation immediately after initiation is the "immediate bestower of nirvāṇa. This [second type], which bestows nirvāṇa not immediately [but upon death], belongs to whom?

To explain why it should be performed, he says: "For children, fools, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual pleasures, and those afflicted by disease, there may be a seedless initiation (nirbījakā dīkṣā), devoid of the rules of conduct (samayācāra). 'Children' refers to those who have merely been initiated; 'fools' refers to the ignorant."
"Stupid, foolish, and ignorant"—thus says Amara. "The aged" refers to women afflicted by old age;
"the devoted" refers to those who enjoy worldly pleasures, being tormented by their longing for sense objects.

For those who are diseased—whose bodies are afflicted by diseases such as consumption or leprosy and who have failed in their vows—the initiation is "seedless" (*nirbījakā*). That initiation, however, bestows purity through the observance of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*). For children and others, initiation occurs at that very time because they lack the capacity to perform the practice of the rules of conduct.
The conduct of the *samaya* is that by which [impurities] are drawn out and purified by the teacher from their respective domains through the power of various methods; therefore, it bestows purity.
And so it is said in the *Vṛddhajñānaratnāvalī*: "The [initiation] for children and others..."

It has been stated that [initiation] which bestows liberation without depending on the performance of rules (*samaya*) and so forth is called "independent" (*nirapekṣā*) or "seedless" (*nirbījā*). It is said: "That which is independent is so called because it does not depend on those [rules] for individuals such as the highly deluded or the very young who are incapable of observing the rules and so forth."
"It is concluded. Now, he speaks of that which has a seed (*sabījā*), which is synonymous with "dependent" (*sāpekṣā*): "And for the wise and the capable, it is proclaimed as having a seed.
For the wise, who possess knowledge of the scriptures, and for the capable, through the performance of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*).

And for those who are capable, that [discipline] which possesses seeds and is dependent on others is proclaimed as the "highest" (para); the word "should be performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And so it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Together with the performance of the observances (*samaya*) and so forth, and with the personal virtues such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)..."
That [volition] which is dependent on factors residing in a person (*puruṣagata*) is called "dependent" (*sāpekṣā*) and is designated as "with seed" (*sabīja*).

And it has been said: "That which leads one toward all goals, follows the timing of the basis (*ādhāra*), and consists primarily of distinguished qualities of the self—that is called 'dependent' by the wise."

838) Now, he also states that even the *sabījā* [initiation] is of two kinds, according to the distinction of its objects: "The *sabījā* is divided into two; the first is that which possesses the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*). It is said to belong to the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*)."
Due to the distinctions of place, time, and so forth.
Initiation with seed (*sabījā-dīkṣā*) is divided into two types. Among these, the first is that which possesses the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*);
it pertains to both the seeker (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), and varies according to differences in place, time, and so forth.
The definition of the place is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "A sacred ford (*tīrtha*) situated on the bank of a river..."

Near a meritorious forest, or near a sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) or a temple of Śiva, in a house that is auspicious, one should construct a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) in a place that has been purified and cleansed. The characteristics of the initiation pavilion have been described by us in the *Kṣārādeśa*.
Let that which has been elaborated there also be maintained here.

Time, however, is precisely the time of the varying degrees of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*); for this very reason, it is by virtue of the varying degrees of the descent of power that there are various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*), such as *sadyonirvāṇa* and others.
It is possible. Alternatively, the times mentioned by Trilocanaśiva and others may be adopted.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
"In the time [of the year] when the months of Pauṣa and Caitra have been removed from the annual [cycle], during the festival of the deity and the seat, [the days of] the transits [are to be taken]."

"During the equinoxes, the solstices, the eclipses, the initiation (dīkṣā), the Pavitra festival, and on the days of Maitra, Ārdrā, Anila, Saumya, Paitṛka, Nirṛti, the one called Pūṣan, Śāṅgīśvara, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttarās— excluding Tuesday and Sunday. Thus it is said.

Thus, having reflected upon the various past and future karmas consisting of the nature of Śiva-dharma, that [state] wherein they are purified is called Dharmiṇī; having mentioned the object, she describes its essential nature as follows: "She who possesses the nature of Śiva."

"Previously accumulated" means gathered in the past. "Future" refers to that which is to be experienced in this life or in another birth, consisting of merit and demerit— that is, having the nature of virtue and vice— and being manifold.
Having reflected upon all the various kinds of karma through the mind and having delineated them,

it is stated that the initiation (dīkṣā) which possesses the nature of Śiva and Śivadharmiṇī renders [the soul] capable of producing its fruit by means of offering oblations corresponding to each specific enjoyment, wherein the portion of whichever [karma] is to be exhausted is [removed].

He states the essential nature of the *lokadharmiṇī* [power]: "The second is the *lokadharmiṇī*, for the purification of mere unrighteousness (*adharma-mātra*).
