Having established the karma of mere righteousness (*dharma-mātra*) for the sake of existing enjoyments in various worlds and so forth, [he speaks] of mere unrighteousness—that is, of all unrighteous acts.

When purification has been performed in the manner previously described, the word "mother" (mātṛ) refers to that capacity; this is the second initiation, known as the "worldly" (lokadharmiṇī), which possesses seeds.
Therefore, it consists of dharmas for the sake of enjoyment in various worlds within the worlds, according to their respective requirements.
In this [state], the quality of being Śiva exists;

because the nature of Śiva exists within her, she is called "Śivadharmiṇī" (She who possesses the nature of Śiva). This initiation possesses its true meaning, and it is twofold according to the distinction between the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*). Among these, the higher is direct.

The former is the cause for attaining the state of Supreme Śiva (paraśivatva). The latter, however, apart from the dissolution of the body, is the cause for attaining the state of Supreme Śiva after enjoying desired objects at will in the worlds of enjoyment by means of a divine body assumed through one's own will.
Likewise, in the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*:
"The individual soul (*aṇu*) who possesses the nature of Śiva is the root of the glory that is the fruit of the dharma of Śiva.
"Even so, others [hold that this is not the case] because the bodies of worldly beings do not perish.

Furthermore, the worldly path (*lokadharminī*) is twofold, distinguished as higher (*parā*) and lower (*aparā*). Among these, the higher is the cause for attaining the state of Śiva only after the body has fallen, for one who has experienced enjoyments within those worlds. The lower, however, is for even those who seek enjoyment.

The *dehottara* bestows the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest. As it is stated in that very same [text]: "When the portion of one's misdeeds has been exhausted across all the planes of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmis*), the *dehottara*—which possesses the worldly attributes desired by the remaining [karma]—is for the sake of [attaining] atomization and the other powers. Furthermore, the powers such as atomization are accompanied by their respective adjuncts (*sāñjanā*).

And therein, there are those who are "stained" (sāñjana) and those who are "unstained" (nirañjana). Those who are stained are perfected through the methods taught in the Yoga scriptures, such as the practice of pouring water at the feet (pādāñjali) and so forth. The unstained, however, are perfected through the power of practicing the Śaiva mantras. As it is said in the Kāmika:
The attainments resulting from desire are to be known as manifold; among them, the attainment of lordship is considered the lowest, while the various supernatural powers (siddhis) are my own domain.
Having practiced the supreme and most excellent conduct, which is equal to that of the gods,
each one possesses many powers, such as the lordship over the sciences (vidyeśatva) and so forth, which are terrifying to others.

The state of a Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), the state of Rudra, the state of Brahmā, and the station of Viṣṇu— the bliss found in the abodes of Rudra, such as those of the Lord of the Immortals (Indra) and others, which are the effects of Māyā.

One should know that the other is supreme, abiding in the state of Ananta and the rest. This concludes the description of the qualified candidates for initiation into both the Śivadharminī and Lokadharminī [traditions],
as illustrated in the Jñānaratnāvalī, as follows:

The initiation into Nirvāṇa is twofold: the worldly and that which follows the nature of Śiva. The worldly is to be known as pertaining to householders, while that which follows the nature of Śiva pertains to those who bear the *liṅga*.
Where there is no cutting of the top-knot (śikhā), that initiation belongs to the worldly order;
where the top-knot is joined with a [specific] portion, that initiation belongs to the order of Śiva.

Likewise, when the principle of Māyā is purified, that initiation in which one burns away the topknot (*śikhā*) is the "Śiva-natured" (*śivadharminī*) initiation, for its measure is the attainment of the nature of Śiva. Any other initiation that does not involve the cutting of the topknot is the "worldly-natured" (*lokadharmiṇī*) initiation.
Thus, there is a twofold division based on the difference in qualification (*adhikāra*) or the difference in subject matter.

Because even the *samayin* and *putraka* possess only the qualification for the obligatory rites (*nitya*), initiation (*dīkṛṣā*) for them is indeed devoid of further qualification; it does not qualify them for occasional rites (*naimittika*). The so-called occasional initiation refers to rituals such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the like.

Since even a *samayin* or a *putraka* who is unfit for the office of an officiant (*karaṇa*) possesses only the authority for daily rites (*nitya*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) for them is indeed without authority—
meaning it is devoid of authority for occasional (*naimittika*) and other such rites; however, he states that for the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya*, it does possess authority.

Because they possess the qualification for all rites— whether daily, occasional, or optional— for both the practitioner (sādhaka) and the teacher (ācārya), that [initiation] is indeed "with qualification" (sādhikārā) for those two,
the practitioner and the teacher, in their daily, occasional, and optional rituals.
Because they possess authority over all rites, that initiation for those two— the practitioner and the teacher— is indeed endowed with authority.
Thus, it is said in the Kālottara:
O Six-faced One, the preceptor must perform the three daily rites and the exposition; for the practitioner, there are the obligatory and optional rites as prescribed in his own scripture.
p.

842) "It is thus proclaimed that this [practice] always applies to both the *samayin* and the *putraka*. Now, regarding the *samayin*, *putraka*, *sādhaka*, and *ācārya*, the difference in their characteristics arises precisely from the difference in their initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Demonstrating this, he says:
"Where there is yoga in the state of Rudra, and where the yogi is in the state of the Lord of Yoga; where there is no cutting of the topknot—that initiation is the Samayī, which is of two kinds."
In that [initiation] where the yoga-disciple is joined to the state of Rudra during the initiation of the rule (samayadīkṣā), that is one;

in that where the yoga-disciple is joined to the state of Īśvara, that is the other—thus that initiation of the rule for the initiate (samayī) is twofold. In the former, there is the cutting of the topknot (śikhāccheda).

The statement "it does not exist" is merely a description of its essential nature from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vastutaḥ*), because in the *samaya-dīkṣā* there is no cutting of the top-knot (*śikhāccheda*); it is not, however, understood as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This is because, in that context, the cutting of the top-knot is not applicable, as it is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) specifically of the *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*. And thus:

One who has been consecrated by the *samaya-dīkṣā* is one who attains the state of Rudra; one who has been consecrated by the distinguished *samaya-dīkṣā* is one who attains the state of Īśvara. Thus, the definition of a *putraka* (spiritual son) is stated. And so, by the mere *samaya-dīkṣā*...

The attainment of the state of Rudra is mentioned; it is also said that through specific commitments (samaya), there is the attainment of the state of Sadīśvara. Now, he states that even initiation for liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā) occurs for the "son" (putraka) disciple, even when devoid of consecration (abhiṣeka).
Where there is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock, and the yoga that leads to the state of Śiva, that indeed is called Nirvāṇa; it occurs for the spiritual son (putraka) through initiation.
In that initiation where there is the severing of the *pāśa-śikhā* (the tuft of bonds),
it is the severing of the tuft of the remaining thread located at the stations of the five *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti*. Where [this occurs]...

And the union with the state of Śiva—that initiation called Nirvāṇa—should indeed belong to the *putraka* (spiritual son). This means it is for his sake. It is not [attained] through consecration (*abhiṣeka*), meaning it is not devoid of consecration. Thus, even one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa without [prior] consecration is a *putra*.

Regarding the initiation of Nirvāṇa as well, he says that by means of the consecration of the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya-mantra*), one becomes a practitioner (*sādhaka*); and by the consecration of all the *vidyās*, one becomes a master (*ācārya*).
Furthermore, that [initiation] is proclaimed for the practitioner through the consecration of the mantra to be accomplished; and [the master's initiation] through all [the *vidyās*].
Through the initiation of knowledge (*vidyābhiṣeka*), it occurs within the sphere of the teacher.

For one who lacks the desire for liberation and seeks instead the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, it occurs through the mantra; and that mantra becomes the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by him. By means of that—

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is proclaimed for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) through consecration by means of a mantra. Thus, the definition is that a practitioner is one who has been consecrated by the mantra to be accomplished. However, that initiation belongs to the domain of the preceptor (*ācārya*) through consecration by all the vidyās—that is, through consecration by all the mantras.
It should be directed toward the Ācārya; thus, the definition "one whose form is consecrated by all vidyās" is stated in the Kālottara.

Having understood this, one should diligently apply oneself to both dissolution (laya) and enjoyment (bhoga). However, if a guru performs initiation without knowing dissolution and enjoyment, [it is fruitless].
The teacher, together with his disciples, shall be cooked in the Raurava hell;
therefore, the preceptor, having exerted himself, should perform the initiation only after full knowledge.

Thus, initiation (dīkṣā), seed-knowledge (bījajñāna), the purpose, and the distinctions among those qualified lead to the conclusion regarding the various types of initiation, starting with the foot-washing water (pādya).

The bestowal of the state of Śiva upon one who has been joined with the purificatory rite of Śiva— whether by means of ritual action (kriyā) or by power (śakti)— is considered initiation (dīkṣā) in every respect.

Because the bestowal of the state of Śiva occurs for one who has been purified by the rite of Śiva preceded by the *avakuṇḍa* and *maṇḍala* rituals, or for one who has received the purificatory rites of Śiva— whether with or without a formal substratum (*sādhikaraṇa* or *niradhikaraṇa*)— therefore, as previously stated...

Initiation (dīkṣā), which is divided into many types such as the Cākṣuṣī and others, is intended for all bound souls (paśus) who are classified into three categories—sakala, pralayākala, and vijñānākala—in accordance with the descent of power (śaktipāta) or the requirements of their respective capacities for spiritual authority (adhikāra). Such is the meaning of initiation. Thus [regarding] initiation...

Having explained [the teaching], he concludes by granting the fruit: "The embodied soul is liberated from the threefold bond of worldly existence through initiation. By the word "dehī" (the embodied soul), the singular number is used to denote the entire class [of beings].
Even the threefold animal (paśu) is [liberated] from the threefold bond of worldly existence, which consists of *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*.
He is released from the snares of saṃsāra and becomes liberated.
Furthermore, through knowledge or through ritual action, one should purify the teacher and the disciple in the Vāmadeva [mantra].

Now, in order to describe how even the thorough knowledge of the purification of the paths (*adhvan*) is the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*), he says that this path is sixfold: "And that initiation is the complete purification of the paths;
and that path is declared to be sixfold."

The initiation that liberates from saṃsāra consists of the purification of the paths (adhvan). That path, which is of the nature of purification, is an ancillary part of initiation; and that path is traditionally said to be sixfold.
He indicates those very same categories according to the sequence of withdrawal: the path of mantra, the path of words, the path of phonemes, and that which consists of the worlds.
The path of reality (tattvādhvan) and the path of limited powers (kalādhvan) constitute the twenty-one auspicious steps.
The sixfold path (adhvan) consists of mantra, word, phoneme, world, principle (tattva), and aspect (kalā).

The meaning is that during initiation (*dīkṣā*), we reach that single, supreme, primary, and auspicious state called the *Śivatattva* all at once. Likewise, during initiation, the six categories (*ṣaḍadhvan*) beginning with mantra are purified by being condensed into the *Śivatattva*.

Once [the bondage] has been severed, like seeds burnt by fire, they no longer possess the capacity for rebirth and enjoyment; from this it is understood that for those liberated through Śaivism, liberation consists in the manifestation of the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and union (*saṃyojana*), wherein the Śiva-principle alone is recognized as the supreme reality. Such a liberated one [remains] during the process of creation.

"O Lord, come to those who desire the city [of liberation]"— by these words of the King of Beasts (Śiva), because they do not turn back from the Śiva-tattva, their state is indeed supreme liberation, characterized by the absence of return.
Furthermore, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), beginning with Mantra and so forth, should be contemplated as being progressively more pervasive.

He explains the manner of that pervasion, stating that purification must be performed: "The mantras are pervaded by the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the *pradānas*; those [worlds] are pervaded by the *varṇas*; those *varṇas* are pervaded by the *bhuvanas*;
and those *bhuvanas* are pervaded by the *tattvas*. Those *tattvas* are pervaded by the *kalās*."
Having pervaded these here through the sequence of the Kala-cycles,
the mantras— five each, containing the four [levels] within them— are thus to be purified within the *vibhāvas*.
Words are pervaded by [phonemes], and words by phonemes; phonemes are pervaded by worlds, and worlds by principles (*tattvas*); and principles are pervaded by *kalās*.
Thus, even the five *kalās*, which are divided into the five paths (*adhvan*) in due order, should be contemplated and purified. As it has been said:

Here, indeed, the mantras are pervaded by the words, the words by the syllables, those syllables by the worlds, and those worlds likewise by the principles (tattvas), according to the Trilocanaśivācāryas.
This is the relationship of the pervader and the pervaded.
The digits (kalās) here consist of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader; by them, these [entities] are grasped.
In order to demonstrate that the five *kalās* indeed contain the five paths (*pañcādhvan*), he also states their locations for purification:
"Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti are in the ether (*nābhasa*); [the fifth is] Kalā."
In sequence, ending at the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma.
Here, by the term "ethereal" (*nābhasi*), the state Beyond Peace (*śāntyatītā*) is meant, because it is connected with that [state].
These— namely Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā—
are situated in sequence within the heart, throat, palate, brow, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), respectively.

The grammatical connection is that [the elements] are to be purified after having been meditated upon in their respective locations. Now, he describes in sequence the method of abbreviation for the purpose of purifying the five principles (tattva) and so forth within the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti.
Upon cessation, the earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*) alone is to be contemplated as the patient and imperishable; however, for those beginning with Time (*kāla*),
there are one hundred and eight cities.

From the final word up to the word *mahādeva* in reverse order, there are twenty-eight pervasive words (*vyoma-vyāpi*). By enumeration, these two mantras beginning with *sadyojāta* are proclaimed as the Heart (*hṛdaya*). [The qualities] from smell (*gandha*) to sound (*śabda*) constitute the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahma*).

The cause is as follows: in the state of cessation (*nivṛtti*), within the *nivṛtti-kalā*, there is the single earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*), which is the earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*). It is to be contemplated and meditated upon within for the purpose of purification.
In this path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the syllable is the letter *kṣa*. In the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*)—

The hundred and eight worlds beginning with Kālāgni constitute the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvā). Starting from the word *anya* up to the word *mahādeva*, there are twenty-eight words in reverse order, counted from the word *vyomavyāpin*.

This is the path of the word (*padādhvā*). The two mantras are the *sadyojāta* and the *hṛdaya*. The path of mantra (*mantrādhvā*) consists of [the elements] beginning with smell and ending with sound; the qualities (*guṇas*) are smell, form, touch, and sound. Brahmā is the Lord of the Cause (*kāraṇeśvara*). Now, [does this occur] in the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], or in the twenty-four [tattvas]?

The purification of the principles (tattva) is stated immediately thereafter. Therefore, how is there a summary of the elements from smell up to sound within the Nivṛtti-kalā? It is said: in that case, the summary is by way of their being principles (tattva), whereas here it is by way of their being qualities (guṇa).

There is no contradiction. But [it may be objected]: "In this case, it is not appropriate to include the qualities such as smell (*gandha*) within the summary of Brahman and the Lord who is the cause, because they lack the nature of being paths (*adhvan*)."

If it is argued that this [process] is indeed the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*), that is true; for when the *pṛthivī-tattva* is purified, those things connected to it are also to be purified. Even so, since smell and the other qualities are to be purified, they are included [within that]. But how can the Lord who is the cause (*kāraṇeśvara*) reach the state of Śiva?
This is solely for the purpose of favoring and assisting the self without obstruction. Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not for the sake of purification that the earth-tattva is predominant?
Next, he describes the method of condensation within the *pratiṣṭhā* level: "In *pratiṣṭhā*, from *badhinī* onwards, there are twenty-four [units]."
The principles ending with Prakṛti, numbering twenty-three, are to be known as being of the nature of the vowels; the consonants from Ca to Ha are to be known in reverse order.
Furthermore, the fifty-six cities beginning with Amareśa are to be known.
There are twenty-one words beginning with Maheśvara and ending with Arūpa; there are two mantras, Śiras and Vāma, and four are remembered as the Guṇas.
From the *rasas* up to the word (*śabda*), Viṣṇu is the cause here; the explanation is provided by the *nigada* itself.
Now, he describes the method of condensation within the *vidyā-kalā*: "In the *vidyā*..."
The seven principles, beginning with Puruṣa, are to be known in their proper sequence, as well as the twenty-seven worlds, beginning with Vāmā.

The meditations are for the purpose of sustenance, extending to the limit; from the first word onwards is the pervasive [mantra]. There are twenty mantras of the words, established as the terrible *śikhā* [mantra].
The seven letters beginning with *ṇ* and ending with *v* in reverse order [correspond to the elements]; form, touch, and sound are their qualities, and Rudra is the cause.
This also is to be explained as before.

Now he describes the method of abbreviation for the *śāntikalā*: "In the *śānti* [kalā], however, there are three principles (*tattva*s): Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and the three phonemes ga, kha, and ka."

The two mantras are Vakratuṇḍa and Vighnāntaka. Previously, there were eighteen [mantras] by way of enumeration, beginning with "Nityaṃ yoginaḥ" and so forth, and ending with "Vyomavyāpi naḥ"; these eleven words have been stated here in reverse order. And [there is] "Guṇāsparśaḥ."

And Sound (Śabda) and the two [others], namely Īśvara, are the cause; this has already been explained in detail. Now, he describes the method of summary regarding the Śāntyatīta-kalā: "In the Śāntyatīta-kalā, however, the Śiva-tattva is established; elsewhere, [the tattvas] beginning with Nivṛtti [are located]."

There are fifteen [syllables] beginning with *bhava*. In the mantras, *om* is one word; *astra*, *īśāna*, and *śiva* are three. Alternatively, the syllables ending in *a* following the *visarga* are proclaimed as sixteen.
*Bhava* is one; the *guṇas* are the cause of sound, while Sadāśiva is the cause of the word. This too—
This is indeed a word-for-word commentary (*nigadavyākhyāna*),
because a detailed explanation of these [terms] is possible precisely according to the sequence of locations that will be described.

Having thus explained the method for summarizing the paths (adhvan), he says that the principles of Śakti and Śiva are also to be meditated upon: "Having thus contemplated the path, and having then meditated on the Supreme Śakti who pervades the six paths, one should meditate on the supreme state above her."
Having contemplated and meditated upon the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) according to the previously mentioned brief method—

where the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacana*)— and then, immediately thereafter, having meditated upon the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) which pervades the path of letters (*varṇādhvan*), above that...

One should contemplate the supreme state above Parāśakti—the state known as Śivatattva, which is synonymous with dissolution (laya)—as the very place where the liberated souls abide. The phrase "for the purpose of uniting the disciple" is to be understood as the ellipsis. [Below] the Śivatattva...

The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that in the absence of the correct contemplation (*samyag-bhāvanā*) of all the principles (*tattvas*), the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is indeed difficult to discern. Furthermore, such contemplation must be preceded by correct thorough knowledge, because that which is unknown is difficult to discern. In this regard, this alone is the supreme seed of all initiations (*dīkṣā*).

Having thus explained the manner of the condensation of the paths (*adhvan*), he now makes a formal declaration in order to state that since the condensation of the paths is impossible without a thorough knowledge of their essential nature, those very paths and their divisions which are employed in initiation (*dīkṣā*) are precisely these [that have been described]. Now, regarding those [paths] employed in initiation...

The enumeration of the extent of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) is stated in due order according to their respective divisions; "is stated" means it is explained by way of classification. Therein, he states the division of the path of mantra (mantrādhvan):
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, Īśāna, Vṛkṣaśiras,
Śikhā, and Varma— these are proclaimed as the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) at the root of the thread.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna, along with the mantras of the heart, head, crest, armor, eye, and weapon— these twelve, together with the root mantra (mūlamantra),
are proclaimed as the path of mantras (mantrādhvan). Their sequence of support within the causal realm (kāraṇa) is as follows:

In the sixteenth vowel, excluding the neuter ones, combined with the syllable known as Nāda which corresponds to the number twelve, and likewise the seventh and ninth letters among those numbering thirty-six (the vowels and consonants).
The five Brahmans, conjoined with Bindu and Nāda, are declared to be Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna, O twice-born ones.
Indeed, the Brahmā-mantras, ending with the word of salutation (namaskāra), follow this very sequence: by means of the second, the fourth, the sixth, and the eighth [syllables].
By means of mantras of ten and twelve syllables, six and eight [limbs] are prescribed:
the heart, the head, the crest, and the armor.
The eye-weapon and the six limbs are proclaimed in sequence; those beginning with the heart and ending with the eye are declared to be joined with the nasal dot (bindu).
The weapon-mantra (astra) extends up to its emission and is endowed with the six classes [of mantras],
following the sequence of *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.

These indeed constitute the sixfold birth-mantra (jāti-ṣaṣṭha), joined with the sequence beginning with *dhṛt* and ending with *astra*; having placed the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning, one should thereafter pronounce the individual syllables.
The fourth-case ending for the *apidhāna* (covering), conjoined with the *namas* and other [salutations],
as well as the high utterance of the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*), is honored in ritual activities; likewise:

In the Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍala, [the seed-syllables] are non-impotent (aklība) in the group of space (vyomavarga), while in the cavities and heads they are the qualities and the moon; [these are] the seeds of Īśa, Puṃs, Ghorā, and Vāmā; one should utter them as short vowels.
In that very same group, the syllables *dṛk*, *veda*, *rasa*, *ibha*, *paṅkti*,
and *mānava* are known as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the heart and the other limbs, respectively.
The sixth [vowel] is quiescent, accompanied by Jambhāri, along with the Bindu and Nāda; Śiva is the mantra, conjoined with the Heart [syllable] and Dhūpa.
Thus, according to the teaching of the Omniscient One, the extraction of the root mantra is as follows:
one should join the sixth seed-syllable to the fifth seed-syllable born in the heart.

One should cause the *bindu* to be placed upon the head, conjoined with the three measures (*mātrā*). One should know Śiva to be of this nature throughout all the phonemes in their proper sequence. Furthermore, regarding the specific application (*viniyoga*), one should arrange the short, long, protracted (*pluta*), and infinite [vowels] according to one's desire. In this regard:
By the word "short" (hrasva), the Brahmans are meant; by the word "long" (dīrgha), the limbs (aṅgas); and by the word "protracted" (pluta), the root mantra (mūlamantra).
The teacher Aghoraśiva has also explained that by the word *ananta*, it is indeed *samananta* [that is meant].
The short [form] destroys sins; the long [form] certainly effects eradication (*uccāṭana*); the protracted [form] is for the attainment of water.

It has been stated that there is a distinction in application (*viniyoga*) such that [the mantra] should be joined with the rites of liberation (*muktikarma*) as being infinite; in that very context, one should employ it in conjunction with worship (*arcana*), ending with the salutation (*namaskāra*).
"Those joined with 'home' at the end are for peace (śāntika), while those preceded by 'ākarṣa' are for attraction (ākarṣaṇa).

I shall now describe those that are to be employed joined with the utterance of 'svāhā' at the end. Thus, indeed, according to the statement of many Āgamas, the Brahmamantras are to be conceived as having short vowels, and the Aṅgamantras as having long vowels.

Since the vowels of the Brahmanas must be short, and according to the rule that there are no short vowels among the semi-vowels (*sadyakṣara*), how can the syllable *oṃ* be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of both Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa? It is replied: as the authors of the *Śikṣā* have said:
Is it not the case that the followers of the *Chāndogya* recite "hastam ekāram" and "hastam okāram" as belonging to the *Sātyamugrīrāyaṇīya* school?

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the path of mantras" (*mantrādhvan*), why are only the root-mantras of the limbs of Brahman mentioned, when there also exist seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantra*)? If this is the objection:

It is true that because one lacks the capacity to purify the seventy million mantras during initiation, and since all of them are included within the *anetra*, they are employed solely for the purpose of purification; therefore, it is these alone [that are purified].

There is no contradiction in stating that the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) is *udyama* (the upward effort). Having thus explained the path of mantra, he describes the essential nature of the path of words (*padādhvan*): "In this way, the path of words is proclaimed to consist of exactly eighty-one words.
Regarding these eighty-one words and their constituent phonemes:
The divisions of this [mantra] and its presiding deities have been set forth in the Siddhāntaśekhara as follows: "Om" is the single syllable; therein, that word shall be the one ending with Śiva.
The second [syllable] is five-colored and is the word for the pervader of space, beginning with the Vaiśyas;
the third shall be the five-colored word for that which has the nature of space.
The fourth [syllable] is five-colored and is the all-pervading state; the three-syllabled mantra "śivāya" and the words for the five limbs [are also included].
"Anantāya" is the four-syllabled designator of Ananta; "Anāthāya" is the four-syllabled term for Sūkṣma.
For Anāśrita, the five-syllabled mantra taught by Śiva is non-denotative; and "dhruvāya" is the three-syllabled denotative mantra of Ekanetra.
To the eternal one, the eight-syllabled mantra which denotes the four castes as one with Rudra;
to the three-formed one, established upon the seat of yoga.
The five-syllabled station of Śrīkaṇṭha is eternal for the yogin;
that five-syllabled designator of Śikhaṇḍin serves as sustenance through meditation.
Oṃ, *namaḥ śivāya* is the word for Śiva; the six-syllabled mantra is that of Gāyatrī, and the five-syllabled mantra is that of Sāvitrī—the word for the source of all.
The three-syllable mantra "Śivāya" is used in the worship of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras),
while the six-syllable mantra "Īśānamūrdhāya" belongs to Īśāna.
The seven-syllable mantra for Tatpuruṣa is "tatpuruṣavaktrāya," and that of Bahurūpin is "aghorahṛdayāya," also consisting of seven syllables.
The seven-syllable mantra "syādvāmadeva guhyāya" belongs to Vāmadeva; the seven-syllable mantra "sadyojātamūrtaye" belongs to Sadyojāta.
"Syād oṃ namaḥ namas tu syāt"—this five-syllable mantra is the expression of Caṇḍa.
Then follows the six-syllable heart-mantra: "guhyātiguhyāya."

The two syllables *goptre* are considered to be the designators of its head; the four-syllable word *śikhāyai* should belong to the crest, and the word *nidhanāya* is considered [the designator] of the base.
The armor-mantra consists of seven syllables: *sarvavidyādhipāya*. The weapon-mantra is the five-syllable word *jyotirūpāya*.
The eight-syllable Netra-mantra is declared to begin with Parameśvara; furthermore, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of Caṇḍanātha for Parā have been proclaimed.
"Acetanācetanā" is its seven-syllable seat; "vyoma" and "vyomapada" are to be known as the four syllables of Dharma.
The syllable *vyāpinyāpiny* is four-colored and denotes that knowledge;
likewise, *arūpinnapyarūpinyai* is the six-syllabled mantra of detachment (*vairāga*).
The six-syllable mantra "Prathama Prathama" represents sovereignty; "Tejas Tejas" consists of four syllables and is the word denoting the pericarp (karṇikā).
The light of the infinite one is considered to be the fourfold color; above and below the filaments, the station is considered to be thirty-two.

Then there should be the word *arūpa* (formless), followed by *anagni* (fireless) and *adhūma* (smokeless); then the word *abhasma* (ashless), and then *anādi* (beginningless), *cātha* (and then), *nānānā*, and likewise the word *dhūdhūdhū*.
These seven steps are auspicious in the Śiva-āgama:
"Oṃ Bhūḥ" is a two-syllable mantra, and "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ" is a three-syllabled one.
Oṃ, *svovarṇadvayaṃ* and *anidhana* consist of four syllables; *nidhana* should be known as three syllables,
while *nidhanodbhava* consists of five syllables.
The syllable *bhyakṣara* is considered to be *Śive*, which comprises all words; the syllable *bhyakṣadyakṣara* is *Paramātman*; and *Maheśvara* consists of four syllables.
O Mahādeva, the four castes are the expression of the Lord of True Being;
the four castes are great splendor—the state that rests upon the feet of the Lord of Yoga.
The five-syllable word "muñca muñca" is considered a four-syllable [mantra] term;
likewise, "pramatha pramatha" is said to be a six-syllable term.
O Śarva, O Śarva, you who know the four castes as they truly are; O source of existence, you who manifest the four castes and bestow happiness upon all beings.
The eight-syllable mantra brings about the presence of all; the seven-syllable one is as follows:
"arcitā arcita" (worshipped, worshipped), referring to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who are supreme.

The "unfamiliar" (asaṃstutā) is [the same as] the "familiar" (saṃstutā), and the "previously situated" (pūrvasthitā) is likewise previously situated; these are the eight syllables and four words in the Śiva-āgama.
There should also be thirty-two filaments and their bases according to the tradition;
the word "sākṣin" (witness) repeated four times shall be the term denoting the petals.
The eight steps of Indra and the others will be explained in sequence as follows: *caturvarṇaṃ turu turu* six times, and *pataṅgapataṅgavai*.
Piṅga, piṅga, the fourfold color; jñāna, jñāna, so it is considered; śabda, śabda, the fourfold color; sūkṣma, sūkṣma, likewise the word.
The three-syllable mantra *śiveti* consists of all feet and pervades the eight directions; it is considered the three-syllable mantra consisting of all words,
presiding over all the quarters.
"Namaḥ" is the five-syllabled word considered the Brahman of the head; "Oṃ Śivāya" is the four-syllabled word expressive of Rudra.

Salutations, salutations! The state of the four aims of life is considered the goal in the Pāśupata system; the single syllable "Om" is to be meditated upon, and it is the designator of the cow-pen and other such places.
The path of words (padādhvan) is proclaimed to consist of three hundred and eighteen syllables and eighty-one words; thus it is fully described.

Thus, having first established the explanation of the verses in the *Śivatanuvarṇanapaṭala* of the *Kālottara* in six thousand [verses], the number of syllables in that [mantra] was subsequently set forth at the very beginning of the *Śivasadbhāvapaṭala*.
For example,
the number of syllables spoken by Śiva is three hundred and sixty-eight; this is the secret mantra that has issued forth from Śambhu.
And it has been stated previously that the meaning of the mantra arises through the Vidyeśa.
Now he describes the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan):
"The path of phonemes is proclaimed as beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'. This...

The explanation has already been given. Now, by means of describing the inclusion of the paths of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) within the principles (*tattva*), he states a summary according to their own measure and limits:
The worlds of Kālāgni, Rathakūśmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava,
and Draura are situated as the six [regions] within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The skull-bearer, the praised, the unborn, the awakened, the diamond-bodied crusher, the pervasive lord, the imperishable teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the sovereign of the thirty gods.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana,
Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka.
Yama, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, and likewise Vidhātṛ; the Maker, the Joiner, and the Separator;
Dharma, and likewise Dharmapati.
Nirṛti is the slayer and killer, with a cruel gaze and terrifying appearance;
he has smoke-colored hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and reddish fangs.
Bala and Atibala, the mighty Pāśahasta, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghahasta, and Jalāntaka.
Meghanāda and Sunāda are proclaimed as the tenth;
[the others are] Śīghra, Ulkhu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, and Kṣayāntaka.

The ender of the five, the one with five locks of hair, the one with matted locks, he whose vehicle is the clouds; the lord of treasures, the handsome one, the blessed one, the one of perfect body, the wearer of matted hair.
Lakṣmīdhṛk, Rattadhṛk, Śrīdhṛk, and Prasāda;
Vidyādhipa and Īśa, who are omniscient, possessing wisdom, and having reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Smareśa, Śarva, Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla, Balipriya, Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and Mārutāśana.
Grasta, Udumbarīśa, Phaṇīndra, Vajradaṃṣṭrin,
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Triyakṣa, Astra, and Daśeśvara.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabhas, Lupsu, Trilocana, Vīrabhadra,
and Bhadrakālī— above all these are two worlds.

Since these verses are in the form of instructions (*upadeśa*), the meaning is easily established merely by the word-division (*padaccheda*). Now, regarding those [verses] mentioned at the beginning, it was stated: "First, six [are placed] in the middle of the Brahmāṇḍa. Others, however, [place them] in the ten directions starting from the east, such as *prāc* and so forth.
He effects the division by including the ten Brahmāṇḍas and the two worlds above them: "The ten beginning with Kapālīśa are in the east; Agni, Rudra, and the others are in the southeast;
those beginning with Yama are in the southern quarter; and those beginning with Nirṛti are in the southwest."

Balā and the others are in the western quarter; Śīghra and the others are in the domain of Vāyu (the north-west); Nidhīśa and the others are in the north; and Vidyādhipa and the others are in the north-east.
Vṛṣa and the others, however, are enjoyers [of the fruits] below you; Śambhu and the principal ones are situated above them, in the ten directions outside the Brahmāṇḍa.

Now, within the *nivṛtti-kalā* itself, he withdraws one hundred and eight worlds, beginning with Kālāgni. Thus, by the enumeration of the ancient cities headed by Kālāgni, it should be known that there are one hundred and eight [worlds] within the *nivṛtti* and other *kalās*.

Having thus described the worlds situated within the principles (tattvas) existing in the *nivṛtti* and *kalā* levels, [the author] now states the worlds existing in the *pratiṣṭhā* level, beginning with *aprākṛta*.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimīśa, Puṣkara, Auṣadha,
Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa, as well as Bhārabhūti and Lakulīśvara.
Then Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Lokpīśa, Āmrādi-keśvara, Madhyameśa,
Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
Gayā, Gurukṣetra, Nākhalo, Nakharu,
Vimaleśa, Uṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmakeśvara;
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, the mighty Ravimukta, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa,
Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as well.
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara,
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Staleśvara, and Thaleśvara.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yakṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya,
Prājāpatya, and Brāhma— these are to be known as the eight [forms of marriage].
The Akṛta, the Kṛta, the Bhairava, the Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Cauma,
and likewise the Śrīkaṇṭha as the eighth.
Thus, having thus indicated the names of the worlds situated there within the *Pratiṣṭhākālāvarta*,
he makes the division into fifty: those beginning with Amareśa belong to the principle of *Āptatva* (the Attained),
and those beginning with Hariścandra belong to *Tejas* (Energy).
Gayā and the others are in the element of air, while Vastrā and Padā are in space;
Chagalaṇḍa is in the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra), and Paiśānī and the others are situated in the earth.
