861) Thus, the fifty-six cities beginning with Prakṛta and Kṛta should be known in the context of installation (pratiṣṭhā) by means of the names of the days starting from Amareśa.
And here, O Cāmara, the [eight] beginning with Śāda, as well as those known as the Atiguhyāṣṭaka, Guhyātiguhyāṣṭaka, Guhyāṣṭaka, Pavitrāṣṭaka, and Sthāṇvaṣṭaka,
have been proclaimed by the command of the Supreme Lord for the sake of favoring the worlds; they dwell upon the earth and exist in the form of liṅgas.
Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The eight Rudras of the primary secret (*ādiguhya*) and likewise the eight of the supreme secret (*atiguhya*)."
The Guhyāṣṭaka, which is more secret than the secret, and also the Pavitrāṣṭaka.
These five—the Sthāṇus and the Aṣṭakas—dwell upon the earth by command; they are established as manifest forms (liṅgas) for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
Whatever water is situated near them, O Six-faced One, that is a supremely meritorious holy site (tīrtha); having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva.
Those men who always give up their lives in these places,
having burst through the shell of the universe, go to the state of the fifty-eight [deities].

Furthermore, liberation resulting from bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), residing in holy shrines (*śivakṣetra*), and so forth, is merely inferior liberation (*aparamokṣa*). Superior liberation (*paramokṣa*), however, arises only through initiation (*dīkṣā*); it does not exist apart from initiation, as has already been established previously.
Now, [the scripture] describes the worlds existing within the wick of knowledge and art (vidyā-kalā):
Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna, Eka-vīra, Pracaṇḍa,
Māpatī, Aja, Ananta, and Eka-śiva.
Krodha, Caṇḍodyuti, Saṃvarta, Lakulīśvara,
Pañcāka, Ekavīra, Śikhoda, and Mahādyuti.
Vāmadeva, Udbhava, Bhava, and also Ekapingala; likewise Ekekṣaṇa, Īśāna, and Aṅguṣṭhamātraka.
Now he makes their division according to the distinction of the principles (tattva): the group of five beginning with Vāmā [is located] in Puruṣa, and the group beginning with Pracaṇḍā in Rāga.
In Niyati and the others, there are Krodha and the rest; in Mahādyuti and the others, there is Mādhika; and in the Vidyā of the ancient Puras such as Vāmā, there are twenty-seven.
Now, regarding the worlds of the Śāntikalā, he says: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī,
Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, and likewise Balapramathanī.
Sarvabhūtadamanī, Manonmanī, Anantaka, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Rudra, and Trimūrtika.
Śrīkhaṇḍa, Śikhaṇḍī, and likewise another, Sadāśiva; these are the eighteen worlds belonging to the Śānti-kalā, beginning with Āmamukha.

Here, within the sphere of the world, the Śāntikalā is [designated] by the term *manonmanī*. Within the principle of *vidyā*, there is the group of eight beginning with Ananta, ending with *manonmanī*. Within the principle of *īśvara*, there is Sadāśiva alone.
Now, regarding the worlds beyond Śānti, he says (p.
"Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti."
Śāntyatītā, Indhikā, Dīpikā, and likewise Rocikā.
Mocikā, Ūrdhvakā, Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpiṇī, Anantā, as well as Nāthanāśritā and Parā.
Beyond Nivṛtti and the other kalās, there are fifteen cities.
The nature of Nivṛtti and the others is as described in the Mṛgendra-tantra:
"Just as [the Lord] effects the closing of the eyes, so too does He effect the withdrawal of the light of the human soul by means of the Yāmya-śakti (the power of restraint)," and so forth.
He is the consciousness and the sovereign lord of all worlds.
That by which she causes beings to turn back is her "Nivṛttikā" (the one who turns back); "Nivṛtti" is her abode, and therein even the Lord is possessed of cessation.
For one who has turned back, the movement toward the former state is repeatedly characterized by its absence;
that which is checked is the foundation, and he who possesses that is its Lord.
Having abandoned the objects perceivable by the senses, that which imparts knowledge to the individual soul (aṇu) is Vidyā;
she is his bath, and Vidyeśa is her lord.
That by which Hara effects the pacification of all suffering for her is peace (śānti), and that state is also peace; by performing that [act], he too is possessed of peace.
By means of this [knowledge], the worlds of sense-objects are drawn upward; and he who is great, greater, and greatest is made so, and the one who has transcended the mind is liberated.

Those states beginning with *indhikā* exist in all three [stages]; even though there is the possession of qualities such as omniscience, there remains a state of being subject to application due to the presence of impurities (*mala*).
She by whom [the body] is cleansed is his liberator, as is that state; the liberator is the action thereof,
and through the *kūrca* mantra, he makes [him] Īśāna.
The upward-moving [path] is that state, and its Lord is the upward-moving Master; those who have attained that state through the application of Śaiva practice are likewise [liberated].
Having reached that supreme state which is the beginning of the end of that stability, they no longer perform creation and so forth, because they are established in their own senses.
Thus, having spoken, he concludes the path of the worlds: "In this way, there are two hundred worlds existing within the five kalās."
Regarding that which was described in the *Dhvani* as "the two hundred and twenty-four worlds":
here, by the phrase "two hundred and twenty-four worlds," it is meant that this number has been described. This is easily understood.
Other worlds mentioned in the divine scriptures are also included within these three;
their purification is possible through this very much cleansing during initiation.
Having thus described the path of the worlds and so forth, he now speaks of the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*).
Now, the thirty-six principles are: earth, water, fire, air, and ether; smell, form, taste, touch, sound, the organs of generation, and wind.
The foot, the hand, the dwarf, that tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear;
the mind, the ego, and the intellect, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
Rāga, Niyati, Vidya, Kalā, Kāla, Mohinī, Vidyā, Īśvara,
Sadākhya, Śakti, and Śiva are thus remembered.
The nature of these principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, is explained by the words themselves; this is according to the Mataṅga [Tantra].

This has been described in detail in the *Sarvajñānottara* and other Āgamas, as well as in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Tattvanirṇaya*, the *Tattvaprakāśa*, and so forth; however, it is not described here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Now he describes the path of the *kalās*:
"Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise the supreme Atītā—these are the five *kalās*; this is the explanation of the *nigama*."
Now, he concludes the seed of initiation (*dīkṣābīja*) which has been established by means of the non-fragmentary [text]:
"The enumeration of the six paths" (*samuddeśaḥ ṣaḍadhvanām*). Thus, the enumeration of the six paths—mantras and so forth—is completed;
the word "of the seeds of initiation and supreme knowledge" (*dīkṣābījaparajñānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus.

In the commentary named Vilocana on the Varuṇapaddhati composed by Gamajñānadeva, an inhabitant of the illustrious Vyāghrapura, the first section, the Chapter on Initiation (Dīkṣāprakaraṇa), is concluded. Now,
having established the seed-syllable of initiation, [the author proceeds] to the seed-syllable of consecration (Pratiṣṭhā) in accordance with the order of the topics.

Having explained the installation, he states the definition of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): "The offering of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) into the *liṅga*, which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is that of the pedestal (*pīṭha*)."

The installation according to the prescribed rite is fivefold; it is indeed the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) which is the essential nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*). Within that *liṅga*, there is the pedestal (*pīṭha*), whose essential nature is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
The offering according to the ritual of the *piṇḍikā* by way of the path of action taught in the Śiva scriptures is "perfect offering" (*samarpaṇa*). This alone is "yoga," which is a connection.
"Installation" (pratiṣṭhā) is thus expressed; this is the meaning of the sentence.

And this is the general definition [of the rite], wherein the word "offering" (samarpaṇa) refers to the essential nature of knowledge and action by the teacher who knows the established tenets of the Śiva doctrine.

Through skill in thorough knowledge (*parijñāna-kauśalya*), the fetter is seen as auspicious; however, if its true nature is not thoroughly known, that very fetter becomes a thorn. By this, it is first stated that the power of the teacher's knowledge alone is the seed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-bīja*).

And thus, the distilled meaning is that *pratiṣṭhā* is precisely the union of Śiva’s power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and his power of action (*kriyāśakti*). In reality, the power of knowledge, which is inseparable [from him], is one and the same with respect to all objects; it appears as many, though it remains singular.

They establish Śiva’s status as the creator of all; and since that state is called the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and because the agent is independent— given that agency contains independence within it— there is independence.
The power of will is metaphorically designated as that which effects realization; thus, the power of will is also included within the power of knowledge.
And thus, because Śiva is formless (*amūrta*), it is only knowledge and action that are metaphorically designated as his "form" (*mūrti*).

This "form," being like a form, is indeed partless (*niṣkala*); for this very reason, it makes known that the nature of form consists of the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha*. And so it is, because of its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).
A *liṅga* and an image (*pratimā*) are so called because they cause one to reach, or manifest, Śiva, who is omnipresent and formless.

And this manifestation [of the deity] occurs after the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) performed by a teacher skilled in the acts of knowledge; by this very fact, it is indicated that the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) of Śiva is internal, while the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is external.
It exists. That foundation (pratiṣṭhā), characterized as thus described, is fivefold;
it indicates those very modes as being of five types:
establishment (pratiṣṭhāpana), stabilization (sthitasthāpana), and the application of meaning (arthāpana).
Likewise, the ritual of installation (sthāpana) has also been fully explained.
This is the explanation of the traditional scripture (*nigama*). Regarding these [deities], he states the definition of their respective domains according to the order of enumeration:
"In the case of a *liṅga*, after the installation of the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should be joined; Bāṇa and the others [are installed] separately."
When the seat is worn out or destroyed, [one should act] according to the sequence.

In the case of that *liṅga* in which the placement of the *brahmaśilā* (foundation stone) has already been performed previously, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) being performed is said to be merely a re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhaiva*). Even though a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) may be joined, the meaning is that it is merely a mass (*piṇḍimātra*). In such cases, when [the rite] is being performed on a *bāṇaliṅga* or similar object—

The ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-karma*) is called "establishment" (*sthāpana*). When there exists a separate pedestal (*pīṭha*), the consecration performed upon that [pedestal], such as for one made of metal or precious gems, is called "establishment. When a *liṅga* has become worn out, the performance of the rite is called "the removal of the decayed" (*jīrṇoddhāra*).

The word "in this manner" is to be understood as the ellipsis. That which is performed upon a manifest object, such as an image, is called *āsthāpana* (installation). This has been stated by Trilocana Śivācārya:
"The pedestal is the Liṅga, and Umā-Śiva; the union of these two is declared to be the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration)."
That body, whose nature consists of the act of thorough investigation, is said to be fivefold.
p.

868) In the case of a *liṅga*, such as one made of *brahmaśilā* and the like, when it is situated upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) joined with Śiva, the rite is *sthāpana* (installation); whereas for an image (*bera*), there is *asthāpana* (non-installation) and *utthāpana* (raising). Thus is the procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Regarding the fivefold nature [of the object], such as an image and so forth, he states another characteristic of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): "Wherein the installation of the form (*mūrti*) and the lord of the form (*mūrtīśa*),
accompanied by the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*), occurs eightfold or fivefold— that is consecration."

The ritual procedure: the principles (tattvas) known as Ātmavidyā and Śiva, and the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvaras), namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara—this [rite] is endowed with the placement (nyāsa) of these. Just as there is the placement of the forms (mūrtis) and the Lords of the forms (mūrtīśas), whether eightfold or fivefold; therein, the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis) are as follows:

The lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) range from Earth to the Sacrificer; the five forms (pañcamūrtis) range from Śarva to Bhīma; the five elements are the forms themselves. That ritual procedure (vidhi) is wherein there is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of these, including the five causal lords beginning with Brahmā.
The phrase "it is called the foundation of karma" is the ellipsis to be supplied. The essential nature and the distinction of their objects will be clarified by the author himself later on.
Now, since the thorough knowledge of the extraction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*) is also a seed for the foundation, he states its divisions:

When the portion of Rudra is divided into three parts following the Brahma-line, one should extend the *lakṣma* (mark) downward for two parts as far as the water-receptacle; this occurs when the portion of Rudra, which is the portion for worship,
has been divided and partitioned into three equal parts in accordance with the Brahma-line.

"According to the central line" means beginning from the middle portion. "In both lower parts" refers to even the two lower sections; it is characterized by the presence or absence of water-reservoirs.
One should let it hang down from the top of the *piṇḍikā* up to the upper portion (*bhāga*). One should fix it there; as it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

"The Guru, having divided the height of the *rudrāṃśa* into three parts, should discard the uppermost part. Here, even regarding this division into three, a specific rule is stated for the *dīpta* [type of temple]. It is as follows: "From here on..."

I shall explain the characteristics and the marks of the *brahmasūtra*. Having made it free of flaws, one should place it in the portion for the subjects; the portion for worship should be equal, and one should divide it with portions of fame. The portion for the Vedas belongs to Hari; one should exclude that born under Aśvinī.
"In the tenth [section], one should again draw the lines for the marks using a golden needle.

Here, it should be understood that the "tenth" refers to starting from the top; now he describes the width and depth of the lines of the marks being drawn: "In a portion equal to one-twentieth of the length of the *liṅga*..."

The expansion of the *lakṣma* (auspicious mark) and the lordship (*īśatā*) are determined by the depression of the earth; that line is expanded by one-ninth part. In the length of the *liṅga*, within the extent of the *liṅga*, when divided into twenty-four parts—[specifically] at the twenty-fourth part for the Buddha—it is conceived by the intellect as twenty-four.
The established measurement is as follows:
having divided the length into twenty-four parts (*jināṃśa*), the width of the *lakṣma* (the mark) should be made by taking one part; this is the remainder [of the instruction].
Furthermore, the line of the earth and the position of the chest—that is, the two side-lines of the extension of that line—[should be drawn].

From the ninth part of the middle width— that single part which has been adopted as the measurement for the extent of the *lakṣma* (mark)— one should divide it ninefold; the meaning is that by means of one such part, the width and the depth of the interval between the lines should be made accordingly.
870) Now he states the characteristics of the eyelashes and the lines: "From half the *lakṣma*, two eyelash-lines [are drawn], divided by eight parts in that field; six..."

The meaning is that, due to the error of the eighth part being on the back, and by avoiding its conjunction with the upward [line], two side-lines (pārśvarekhā) should be drawn starting from the lower half of the mark (lakṣmārdha),
beginning from the characteristic mark (lakṣaṇa). In that field, the two side-lines are divided into eight parts according to the desired measure of the field.
Then, having divided that site into eight parts, and having excluded two parts from below— either setting aside six parts or seven parts— one should,
with a cord half the length of the field's measurement, [mark] it like a half-moon.
"One should rotate" means one should perform the rotation until the line of the edge of the vessel meets the line on the back of the liṅga;

such is the meaning of "one should rotate. Having thus stated the general definition of rotation, he states the specific rule for one who desires a continuous flow of wealth: "But when divided by fire... [vahni-bhakte tu]...
In that field, for the sake of the continuity of the marks and prosperity, one proceeds by a sequence of two and a half parts;
"by excluding a half-part below" means that in that aforementioned field consisting of two side-lines, one should divide it into three parts when divided by fire (three). There, below—
By excluding half a portion— that is, having excluded the lower half-portion—

one should [construct] two portions and a half in the sequence of the yuga; this is for one desiring the experience of the marks (*lakṣma*) and liberation according to that measurement, thus it is said.

He states that while the two aforementioned methods are common to both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), they must be performed otherwise when directed toward specific varieties of results, such as subjugation (*vaśya*) or attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*): "This [method] applies to the common procedure; in the case of a difference in the task, it is otherwise."
Otherwise, one should look for another method— that is, a different way— in the scriptures that establish the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*); for here, only the seed of consecration is intended.
Because it is intended to be explained, this extraction of the characteristics is fourfold according to the distinction of the objects.
In the *Dīptatantra*:
"The lattice-window, the buffalo-eyebrow, the bird-beak, and the hollowed-palm shape. The lattice-window..."
The tip of the khadira wood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, but for a Kṣatriya, it is the tip of the palāśa.

For Vaiśyas it is the "buffalo-eyebrow" (mahiṣākṣa), for Śūdras the "tip of the hollowed palms" (karapuṭāgraka), and for all [castes] the "shape of hollowed palms" (karapuṭākāra) which effects the gathering of alms; thus, in the *Kāmika*, the extraction of the nine marks (lakṣmaṇoddhāra) is set forth.
Just as a bud, or like an elephant’s eye, the tip of the *liṅga* resembles a lotus; it has the shape of a plantain bud,
with leaf-like structures at the tips of its trident.

"O twice-born ones, the supreme weapons and missiles of the world-protectors, or the supreme weapon of Śiva, are described for the purpose of the characteristics of the universal Liṅga. This definition also should be seen as stated in that very same place by the term "characteristics of the weapon" (*astra-lakṣaṇa*).

The procedure for shaping the head (*śirovartana*) is also a seed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), yet it was not mentioned by the author [of this work] for fear of excessive prolixity; that [procedure] is as stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"The preceptor and the artisan, together with the [proper] characteristics, [should perform] the shaping of the head."
One should perform that; it is said to be fourfold.
The first [stage] has the shape of an umbrella; the second has the form of a gourd;
the third is like a hen’s egg; and the fourth is like a half-moon.

Having made the *tāra* (thickness) one-sixth part [of the total height], the head of the *liṅga* should be divided into seven parts; having performed the rounding with one part, the middle should be depressed.
This is declared to be in the shape of an umbrella, bestowing all accomplishments; having made the *tāra* (the syllable Om) as six parts, it is fashioned with half of two parts.
It should have the shape of a cucumber, bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation; the hen’s egg [shape] should be made right there with half the width.
"Having divided the *liṅga* into three parts and drawn [the design] with two parts,
this half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is there proclaimed in due order for the sake of liberation.
Having thus stated the extraction of the characteristics in general, he shows the specific arrangement:

The opening of the eyes is the characteristic for the manifest (vyakta) and for both the manifest and unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta). Regarding the lingas that consist of both the unmanifest and the manifest-and-unmanifest, it is stated that the characteristic is indeed the unmanifest. For the manifest [lingas], such as images and the like, the opening of the eyes alone is the characteristic; thus, this characteristic must be performed for the manifest-and-unmanifest facial lingas.

The remainder [of the sentence]. Now, he states that the aforementioned definition must in some cases be avoided: "Not on arrows and the like; not when it is moving; nor there with iron; nor even on one's own son"—this is the completion of the statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). The meaning is that the extraction of the target-mark (*lakṣaṇoddhāraṇa*) should not be performed in these instances.

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra], it is held that this [consecration] is not required for a linga made of gems, nor for one made of metal, even if mobile; nor for a Bāṇaliṅga, nor for one of the Raudra type, nor for those originating from a river or a spring.

In their own forms, the characteristic among those fiery gems is luminosity; whether produced from jewels or from metal, it may or may not be subject to the application of auspicious marks (*lakṣman*).

Having thus shown the *lakṣma* on the *liṅga*, he shows the *lakṣma* on the pedestal (*pīṭha*). The pedestal of the *lakṣma* is in the middle of the aperture, shaped like a vulva (*bhaga*) with its tip pointing upward;
at its base, it is marked by a circular line (*bhramarekhā*) equal to one-third of the aperture itself.

The pedestal (pīṭha) is situated upon the pedestal; it possesses the characteristic mark of a mark, is shaped like a vulva (bhaga) in the middle of the aperture, and has its tip pointing upward. Furthermore, at one-third of the aperture, at the base of that vulva-shaped form, there is a circular line (bhramarekhā). That [pedestal] is endowed with such a circular line at its base.

The grammatical connection is "pīṭhalakṣmaṇam" (the mark of the pedestal). This is the meaning: like the *liṅga*, one should divide the hole of the pedestal into three parts; having set aside the upper part, one should rotate [the lower part] like a horse-ear leaf so that, with the two lower parts, the base takes the form of a vulva (*bhaga*).
The secret [sanctum] should be fashioned with a line corresponding in width and depth to the marks of the *liṅga*, because it consists of *śakti*. As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāgama*:
"The characteristic of its excavation is a cavity in the form of a vulva (*bhaga*), such that it is not visible."
"In the *Kāmika* it is said: 'The supreme [liṅga] consists of the attachment to the three worlds.

And: 'The wise Guru, with a golden stylus, should thus draw the mark upon the pedestal: in the center of the cavity, shaped like a vulva, with its tip pointing upward. Thus [it is done] for the liṅga and the pedestal."

Having performed the smooth extraction and the ritual of sprinkling (*secanādi*) as prescribed by the author of the *Pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*, one should undertake the various ritual procedures (*kriyākalā*).

Immediately thereafter, he describes specifically the locus for the particular nyāsas of the forms and the forms of Tatveśvara, distinguishing them [from the previous]: "The pervasion of the liṅga, the pedestal, and the stone proceeds in order from the principles (tattva) onwards, ending with Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva, as a three-part division."

One should further contemplate: the pervasion of the pedestal-stone by the *liṅga*, the pervasion of the pedestal by the *liṅga*, and the pervasion of the stone by the pedestal; this is to be meditated upon in sequence—this is the distinction.
Immediately thereafter, within those [stones], one should contemplate Śiva and Śakti according to the sequence of the emanation of the *tattvas* starting from the *tattva*.
The pervasion extends up to the end of the *sadeśa* (the pedestal-base), just as the pervasion of the Śiva-tattva is in the *liṅga*,

the pervasion of the Śakti-tattva is in the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the pervasion of the Sadāśiva-tattva is in the stone slab (*śilā*). Furthermore, one should conceive of a three-part division (*trikhaṇḍa*) for each of the *liṅga*, the pedestal, and the stone slab.

One should conceive of it in order to manifest [it]; he states that very method: "Māyā, which is called the power of Śiva-vidyā, possesses the power of space; [it extends] from the location of sound and mind up to the end of the location of Being (sat), sequentially in the liṅga, the pīṭha, and the house.
This is the meaning: the liṅga at the bottom consists of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), while in the middle...
Having thus pervaded [the universe] through the relationship of the pervader and the pervaded— [viewing it] as consisting of Śakti at the end and having the nature of Śiva—

one should meditate upon the three sections within the *liṅga* itself; likewise, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should meditate on that which consists of Māyā at the bottom, the nature of Sadāśiva in the middle, and [Śakti] at the end.
Thus, the pervasion of the three sections within the stone—that is, the *aśman*—consists of the essence of the *Śakti-tattva*.

At the bottom, it consists of the elements beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*) and ending with the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). In the middle, it consists of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) and so forth, ending with the intellect (*buddhi*). At the top, it consists of the principles beginning with the *guṇa-tattva* and ending with *Sadāśiva*. Such is the nature of this [pervasion].
One should meditate upon the pervasion of the three sections;
likewise, in the Kāmika, it is said: "Furthermore, one should conceive of the three sections as extending from Śiva and Śakti down to the intellect (manīṣā)."

Vidyā-śakti extends to the limit of Śiva; Māyā is co-extensive with its own region, as is Śakti; and the Śabda-citta is co-extensive with the limit of its own region—thus, respectively, in the Liṅga, the Pīṭha, and the Āśma. Now, incidentally, regarding the consecration of the Prāsāda, the Heart-vase (Hṛt-kumbha) also serves as the seed for the rite of installation.

In that regard, he also describes the pervasion of the paths (*adhvan*) and the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*): "The pervasion up to the end of the *māyā*-principle is proclaimed as the 'Heart-Pitcher' (*hṛtkumbha*). Furthermore, the path of the three sections extends from the *citta-kalā* up to the end of *māyā*, for the temple (*prāsāda*) which is the constituent part of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)."

The remainder [of the instruction] is that the pervasion (vyāpti) of Māyā-tattva and its end should be meditated upon at the root, middle, and tip of the heart-vessel (hṛtkumbha). The "three-part path" (trikhaṇḍādhvā) refers to the three-part way.
Furthermore, [the pervasion] ending with the digit of consciousness (cittakalā) and Māyā is at the root, within the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), and in the middle.
The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should first conceive of the limit of the *kalā-tattva*, and then conceive of the limit of the *māyā-tattva*. Now,

regarding the temple (*prāsāda*) which is to be invoked as having a form within the heart-vessel (*hṛtkumbha*) as its embodied manifestation, he describes its vertical pervasion and the conceptualization of its three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) with respect to the *puruṣa*.
The state of being three-partite, the cognition of the word, and the person as the limit.

Regarding the person designated as the temple: the state of being three-partite, the conceptualization of the three parts, the cognition of the word, and the person as the limit [occur] respectively at the base, the middle, and the top.

The mention of the "Palace" (prāsāda) and the "Person" (puruṣa) here refers to the limit of the principle of Sound (śabda-tattva) and the limit of the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva), respectively; this is for the purpose of indicating the state of the Pralayākala. Thus, it is said in the Piṅgalāmata: "Having invoked the Ātma-tattva, one should place it within the path of the jar."

The pervasive Lord of Consciousness, who abides as the primordial nature of the self of all beings, whose essence consists in the grace of those [beings'] actions, and who is endowed with the impurity of office (adhikāra-mala).

They say that one should restrain the Māyā-prasūti (the birth of Māyā) which is associated with Niyati and the others, along with Kalā, Māyā, Rāga, and Vidyā, for one who is attached; and they maintain that the temple possesses the nature of Puruṣa because it is a particular form of Śiva, as explained in the Mataṅga, Svāyambhuva, and other scriptures.
This should be understood in detail from the *Jñānaratnāvalī*. Regarding the placement (*nyāsa*) as a protective wall:

the Guru should install a pitcher made of gold, silver, or other materials, raised like a treasure-vessel and filled with gold, jewels, and so forth, just like a *liṅga*. Its height should be one *tāla* or half of that.

Likewise, having fashioned a golden image of a man measuring half the size of a thumb, endowed with all the [proper] features, one should perform the bathing ceremony with the five products of the cow and other substances as previously prescribed; then, between the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (vedikā), one should place the jar, which has become the very embodiment [of the deity], upon a pedestal (kulika).

Having recollected the *puruṣa* who is a *pralayākala*, one should contemplate him as being of a single form— consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*cit*), and mantra— and through the exhaling breath (*recaka*), one should place that *puruṣa*, the Lord of Life, within the retention (*kumbhaka*).
One should then fashion his body in sequence from the *kalās*, the *tattvas*, and so forth.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Kalā (Kalā-tattva).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jñānavid, the lord of the principle of Kalā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to that which effects the manifestation of the state of being the master of Kalā and the state of being the agent for this self; perform, perform! (Kuru kuru namaḥ).

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of knowledge, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of knowledge, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas.

Oṃ hāṃ! You are the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) and the rest; perform, perform the fulfillment of transformations! Homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the principle of passion (rāga-tattva)!

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāmadeva, the lord of the principle of passion (rāga-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to him who effects the fulfillment of the passion for sense objects belonging to this lord of the principle of passion; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of primordial nature.

Salutation to Sūkṣma. Oṃ hāṃ, O Lord of Prakṛti, perform the fulfillment of this transformation; salutation. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Buddhi. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Budha, the lord of the principle of Buddhi. Oṃ hāṃ...

Bestow upon him the lordship of the intellect; awaken him! *Namaḥ*. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ahaṅkṛti, the lord of the principle of ego. Oṃ hāṃ, bestow upon him the lordship of the principle of ego; perform the act of self-conceit (*abhimāna*)! *Kuru kuru*.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of mind (manastattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Candra, the sovereign of the principle of mind. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to you who are the lord of the mind; perform, perform [the functions of] conceptualization and discursive thought. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the two ears. Oṃ hāṃ...

Homage to the Lord of the Ear, Tridaśa! Oṃ hāṃ! Bestow, bestow upon him the state of being the lord of the ear and the quality of perceiving sound; homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the Skin! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Vāyu, the lord of the skin! Oṃ hāṃ! [Bestow] upon him the state of being the lord of the skin...
Make me the grasper of touch, make me, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the two eyes.
*Oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Arka, the lord of the eyes. *Oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to you who possess the lordship of the eyes; make me the grasper of form, make me, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*.
Salutation to the tongue. Salutation to Varuṇa, the lord of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ!
Perform, perform the state of being the lord of the tongue and the function of grasping tastes for this [person]; salutation.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the sense of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the two Aśvins, the lords of the sense of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one who performs the function of grasping the knots of the sense of smell, the lord of the sense of smell; perform, perform [this]! Oṃ hāṃ.
Salutation to Speech. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agni, the Lord of Speech.
Oṃ hāṃ, you who are the Lord of Speech, perform the release of speech; perform it, salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two protectors. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra, the Lord of Protection. Oṃ...

Hāṃ! Protect [him]; grant him the lordship over this and the capacity to grasp the objects of the senses; Kuru kuru, Namaḥ! Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the two feet. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Feet.
Oṃ hāṃ, grant him the lordship over the feet and profound energy; Kuru kuru, Namaḥ! Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Pāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mitra, the lord of Pāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to you who perform the emission of the lordship of Pāyu; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Upastha. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ghanānanda, the lord of Upastha. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to Sound. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Sound, the subtle resonance. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one who effects the filling of space with the sovereignty of sound; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Touch. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Touch, the most powerful.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the filling of the wind for this [element] which has touch as its presiding lord; homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to form! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the sun-like lord of form! Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the filling of the fire for this [element] which has form as its presiding lord; homage!
Homage!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rasa; oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rasādhipa, the giver of water.
Oṃ hāṃ, perform the filling with water for this lord of taste; perform it, perform it! Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇḍa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of Gaṇḍa, to the limb of Gaṇḍa!
Oṃ hāṃ, perform the filling with earth for this lord of Gaṇḍa; perform it, perform it! Homage! Oṃ...

Hām, salutation to Ākāśa. Oṃ hām, salutation to Sadāśiva, the lord of Ākāśa. Oṃ hāṃ, perform, perform the granting of space for me, who am the lord of Ākāśa; salutation. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, [salutation] to the lord of Vāyu.

Salutation to Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Speech; perform, perform the manifestation of this [mantra]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Splendor. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the Lord of Splendor. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Splendor; perform, perform the ripening of this [mantra]. Oṃ hāṃ.
Homage to the Waters! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the waters! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to him who performs the gathering of this lordship over the waters! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Earth!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of the earth! Oṃ hāṃ...
"Perform the maintenance of his sovereignty over the earth, perform, obeisance!"—thus one should install [the mantra]. Alternatively:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lords of the principles beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth, such as Jñānavindu and the rest; Oṃ hāṃ..."

"You who are the presiding lords of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth, perform your own respective functions; salutations! Having thus assigned the principles and so forth, one should assign the channels (nāḍīs) and other elements accordingly: the Udgātṛ priest [should place them] from the center of the bulb (kanda), and Kuṇḍalinī resides at the navel."
Above the navel, in the region of the heart, there is a lotus situated like a lotus.
In its center, resting upon the pericarp, are the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the deity named Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Haḥ;
he is Īśāna, who is to be presided over by him, and possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns.
The Suṣumnā is in the middle, extending from the thumb up to the Brahma-bali;
the Iḍā nāḍī is situated in the left nostril, and the Piṅgalā in the right.
Gāndhārī is in the right eye and Hastijihvā is in the left; Pūṣan should be in the right ear and Yaśasvatī in the left ear.

The Meḍhravalaṃpūṣā channel is situated in the anus, while the Kuhū channel is located in the rectum; Śaṅkhinī should be in the center of the navel, and the vital winds such as Prāṇa reside in the mouth.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Suṣumnā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the vital wind (prāṇavāyu) that flows through Suṣumnā. Such are the mantras. Or else: "Salutation to the twelve channels and to the ten vital breaths."
Or the mantras: one should place Kāla and Niyati upon Māyā, who presides over all.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣaṇa, the lord of Māyā.
Oṃ hāṃ, make his state as the lord of Māyā subject to my power; perform, perform, obeisance.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Niyati. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of Niyati, the Controller. Oṃ hāṃ, perform, perform the act of restraining him who possesses the sovereignty of Niyati; homage. (p. 881)
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāla. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kālarudra, the Lord of Time. Oṃ hāṃ, perform, perform the state of being the Lord of Time, the state of abiding for infinite time; homage!

"A person, having experienced the three principles including the Lord— namely, intellect (*buddhi*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and *māyā*— together with their embodied forms and their presiding deities, and having performed recitation (*japa*), should restrain them. Now, as an incidental topic, [I shall describe] the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is the seed of the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the door and so forth, pertaining to the *liṅga*.
He instructs as follows: "The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the doors, the palaces, and the finials (*cūḍā*) is declared to be like that of the *liṅga*.
This is easily understood through the thorough knowledge of the pervasion of the *liṅga* already mentioned and yet to be described.
Here, "finial" (*cūḍā*) means the spire (*śikhara*); the method for its consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is found in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Just as Śukanāsā, at the conclusion [of her practice], having placed the lotus-foot upon her heart, created a body through yoga within the half-lotus of Śuka’s nose.

Having performed the placement with the *haṃsa* seed-syllable, one should effect protection with the armor and weapon mantras; having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the world-supporters, one should firmly secure that gateway.
Then, having constructed a pedestal with a neck [molded] of *āmalaka* wood,
one should perform the installation there of the *īśacūḍa* [liṅga] as if it were a [standard] *liṅga*.

In that case, there is no removal of the characteristic marks; rather, there is the conceptualization of three segments. Entry is through the upper part of the Brahmā [mandala], and the placement of Śakti, the jewels, and so forth is as before.
"Without the knowledge of ritual action, the rest—such as the placement of the *tattvas* and so forth—is like [the ritual for] a *liṅga*.
In that regard, the installation of the banner (*dhvaja*) must also be performed; its characteristics and the method of its consecration have been explained in detail in the *Aruṇācalotsavapaddhati*.

882) In that very context, one should first determine whether the installation (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*), the lords of the principles (*tatveśvara*), the forms (*mūrti*), and the lords of the forms (*mūrteśvara*) is eightfold or fivefold.
That is the procedure. Regarding what was called "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*), he explains that very thing:

"There, in the portions belonging to Viṣṇu and Īśa, one should sequentially deposit the three *tattvas*, accompanied by their respective Lords of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*), consisting of Self (*ātman*), Knowledge (*vidyā*), and Śiva."

In that regard, within the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa in the *liṅga*, there are respectively the three principles (*tattva*) consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva: the principle of Self (*ātmatattva*), the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

One should install [the deities] accompanied by their respective lords of knowledge (*vidyādhipa*); by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*), a mantra is meant. The meaning is that at the conclusion of the *sparśahoma*, one should install them with their respective mantras. Therein, the *ātmatattva* consists of the twenty-four principles beginning with earth, the *vidyātattva*, and the *śivatattva*, in sequence.
One should install [the deities] together with their respective presiding ignorance (*avidyādhipa*). By the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*), a mantra is meant;

the meaning is that at the conclusion of the *sparśahoma* sacrifice, one should install them with those respective mantras. In that context, the *ātmatattva* consists of the twenty-four principles beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*), while the *vidyātattva* consists of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
There are seven principles (tattvas): the principle of Śiva and the five principles beginning with Vidyā.
He states that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are indeed the lords of these principles; in the Liṅga, they are the lords of the three principles.

Here, the word *liṅga* is also indicative of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and the stone; as it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The installation of the stone at the base of the *liṅga* is accompanied by nine divisions (*bhakti*); [this applies] to the image (*mūrti*)."
The ritual placement of Mūrtīśvara is accompanied by the principles (tattvas) and the lords of those principles (tattveśvaras).
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara reside in the Liṅga through the cognition of the three principles; indeed, the triad of principles is declared to be Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva."
Having thus described the principles (tattva) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvara), he speaks of the forms (mūrti) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara):
"Either eight or five [lords] are themselves to be understood as the protectors of the forms.

The eight forms, consisting of the five elements and water, are determined there by the anusvāra following the word *didhikārya*; among these, he describes the eightfold form for the sake of the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), [referring to] the lords of the forms.
Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind, the moon, and the sky—
these eight forms are to be installed in each section.

Previously, in the places divided into three sections, there were Śarva, Paśupati, and foremostly Rudra, as well as Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the guardians of the eight forms (Aṣṭamūrti).
The analysis of this [text] consists simply in the breaking down of its words; it should be understood that the sequence of completion follows the very sequence of the forms (mūrti).

Regarding the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), one must set aside the arrangement of the forms and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśa); however, for the seeker of enjoyment (bubhukṣu), he speaks of both the pure path (śuddhādhvan) and the mixed path (śuddhāśuddhādhvan).
If it is the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), it is threefold.
Regarding that, first he speaks concerning the seeker of liberation (*bubhukṣu*) on the pure path, from *Śuddhavidyā* up to the *Śakti*: "For the seeker (*sādhaka*) on the pure path..."
In the consecration, however, Ananta and the others are the presiding deities.

In that aforementioned pure path (*śuddhamārga*), which begins with the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) and ends with the principle of Power (*śakti-tattva*), for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who desires enjoyment— such as the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth— and who seeks liberation, there is the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Śiva’s Liṅga.

The word "being performed" (*kriyamāṇām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). The *mūrtipās*, however, are Ananta and the others; the *mūrtis* are indeed those previously mentioned, such as Kṣmā, Vahni, and so forth—this is the meaning of the word "tu" (however/indeed).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that they are to be praised as being placed in each section. He mentions those very ones, beginning with Ananta:
"Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetraka, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. [Śikhaṇḍin.]
The phrase "together with the one named Śikhaṇḍin" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Now, for one who desires to enjoy the path of both the pure and the impure, he says: Within the sound whose nature is pure, extending from Puruṣa up to Māyā, the Rudras of the Mūrtis are to be known,
beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra.

In that [reality] which has the *puruṣatattva* as its beginning and the *māyātattva* as its end— thus consisting of both pure and impure aspects, having a nature that is both pure and impure— the sound [is heard] by the practitioner (*sādhaka*), who desires enjoyment but is devoid of the desire for enjoyment and powers such as *aṇimā*; this is the implied meaning.

The forms beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātṛka are to be understood as those that are to be worshipped and installed; this is the remainder [of the sense]. He specifies them as follows: Aṅguṣṭhamātra, Bhuvaneśa, Īśāna, Ekapiṅgala, Udbhava, Bhava, and Vāmadeva.

The one of great splendor. Having thus described the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) on the path of the pure and impure forms, he now states the Lords of Knowledge on the impure path: "On the impure path, they are established from the earth up to primordial matter (pradhāna): Mūrtipa, the hundred Rudras, the eight [Lords], and those beginning with the ten directions."

In that which is thus described—where the earth-element (*pṛthvī-tattva*) is the beginning and the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna-tattva*) is the end—the sound is impure; the ellipsis is "it is the object for one desiring enjoyment. Within the *nivṛtti-kalā* of the hundred Rudras, there are world-rulers (*bhuvanādhipas*) numbering ten in each direction.
Among those numbering one hundred, [there are] those beginning with the lords of the ten directions.
(p. 885) Now, excluding the two lords of the upward direction, among the eight lords of the directions, those who...

The principal ones are also the lords of those [sections], and they alone are established as the *mūrtipās* (guardians of the forms); this is the settled meaning. Now, he points them out specifically: Kapālīśa, Agnirudra, Yāmya, the one named Nairṛta, Bala, Śīghra, Nidhīśa, and Vidyādhipati is the eighth.

Regarding the desire for worldly enjoyment (*aihika-bubhukṣā*), he states a distinction: in some cases, Indra and the others are considered the lords of the worlds who possess form; they are indeed well-known in certain minor rites as the Bhairavas. In other instances, there is a desire for the attainment of a son and so forth, [directed toward] Indra and the others.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped as lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras). They are indeed well-known;

however, in certain minor rites such as killing (māraṇa) or driving away (uccāṭana), they are to be worshipped as lords of wrath (vairavas). To the question "Who are they?", he says: Asitāṅga, Urū, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta...
Bhairava, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra constitute the eight Bhairavas.

Here too, since it is specifically the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) who are mentioned, the "forms" (mūrtayas) are indeed the eight previously mentioned forms, namely Earth and the rest. Thus, in the system of eight.
Having explained the conceptualization of the forms, he states the distinction regarding the fivefold system:
"In the ritual installation consisting of the five forms, the elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
these are the forms in the *liṅga*, while Brahmā and the others constitute the five forms."

Having thus stated that this [deity] is common to both enjoyment and liberation regarding the matter of worldly enjoyment, he says that there is also a distinction regarding the matter of the desire for liberation: "But for the seeker of liberation, the forms such as Nivṛtti reside in Pratiṣṭhā."
p. 886) Sadyojāta and the others are recorded as the five lords (īśvara) of the *liṅga*.
This is indeed a self-explanatory statement. Thus, having described the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms and the lords of the forms upon the *liṅga*, [the text proceeds].

He states the extension [of this rule] to the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the stone (*śilā*) by saying "it is the same for the pedestal and the stone as well. Thus, the placement (*nyāsa*) is to be performed on the pedestal and on the stone; however, this distinction (*bheda*) is the same [as that previously mentioned]. The meaning is that this is the case for the *liṅga* and so forth.
The word "distinction" (*bhida*) refers to what will be stated hereafter; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "that very distinction [is for the seeker of liberation]."
First, it is said that action (kriyā), knowledge (jñāna), and will (icchā) are considered the sovereigns of the three principles;
the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti) are the sovereigns of the three principles.
They are considered, respectively, to be the sovereign goddesses of the three principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
The remainder [is as follows]. Having thus explained the distinction between the principles (tattva) and the lords (īśvara), he states the distinctions among the Mothers (mūrti):
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jñānā, Cetanā, Balotkaṭā, Dhātrī, and Bahvī are known as the Mothers;
they reside in the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth, both within the sphere of the seats and outside the sphere of the seats.
Regarding the pedestal (pīṭha) and the stone (śilā), the eight powers beginning with Dhārikā are considered to be the presiding deities of the forms (mūrtīśas).
Now, for the practitioner (sādhaka) seeking enjoyment (bubhukṣu), he states that during the installation (pratiṣṭhā), the lords of the forms reside in the pedestal and so forth.
Ananta and the others alone would be [the recipients], having come under the influence of the threefold recitation.

In the case of a seeker who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), regarding the *pratiṣṭhā* [consecration], the meaning is that Ananta and the others—who have come under the influence of the female recitation (*strīpāṭha*)—are indeed the powers of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara-śakti*), namely Ananta and the rest;
they are the lords of the forms (*mūrti-adhīśvara*) to be worshipped. This is the remainder [of the sense].
Having thus explained the distinction in the eightfold scheme, he speaks also regarding the fivefold scheme: "Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānā, and Icchā are intended [as the powers].

On the pedestal and so forth, the lords of the five forms (mūrtīśas) [are to be worshipped]; on the pedestal and so forth, the five Śaktis beginning with Vāmā are to be worshipped on the pedestal-stone; the phrase "the lords of the forms" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, because the pedestal-stone is common to both the liṅga and the image, the image will be described hereafter.

Regarding the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): previously, he stated the specific distinction between the pedestal stone (*pīṭha-śilā*) and the stones for the fierce forms (*ugra-mūrti*). Now, concerning the "fierce" (*ugra*) images—that is, those of terrible appearance—the word *ugra* indicates minor rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

The meaning is: "of those employed for such rites. It is said that, for those [deities], the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśanyāsa) occurs upon the pedestal and the stone according to the sequence of eight and five divisions;
this is the remainder [of the statement]. He states that very sequence:
In the fivefold aspect [of the breath], sleep is the destruction of darkness and delusion, death is the fear of illusion, fever is passion,
and the terrible state is discontent and the absence of fever.

This is easy to understand. Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, I shall explain the placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) for the fierce deities (*ugrārcā*) in their proper sequence: "Tamā, Aghorā, Vimohā, Ācārī, Tīrā, Apajvarā, and Amātā"—thus, for these fierce deities, there is the placement of the forms and the lords of the forms upon the pedestal and the stone.

Having first stated the differentiation, he says that for all five [deities], one should meditate upon the pervasion of the path of principles (tattvādhvan) by the elements from earth up to space within each of the lingas, seats (pīṭhas), and stones,
according to the sequence of differentiation that will be described hereafter.

One should likewise contemplate the differentiation of the forms even within the stones of the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) according to the pervasion of the levels of reality (*tattvādhva*). Thus, by means of the sequence of the differentiations of pervasion that will be explained hereafter, it becomes easily understood; he states that very sequence: "ending with Rāga, Earth, Water, and Time, and ending with Vidyā."
Fire; wind up to Īśvara; the space-linga ending with Śiva; and the earth, the ground.

The form of water (*ambu*) is the element of passion (*rāga*), extending up to the end of the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*). Fire (*hutāśana*) is the form of fire, extending up to the end of time (*kāla*), that is, up to the principle of time (*kālatattva*). Air (*vāyu*) extends up to the end of knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, up to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Space (*vyoma*) extends up to the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*).

The meaning is that one should meditate on the process of pervasion: from the form of space up to Śiva—that is, reaching the limit of the Śiva-tattva—the Liṅga is situated within the Liṅga. Now, he speaks of the Pīṭha:
"From Puruṣa down to Earth, from Kalā down to Water, from Māyā down to Fire, and from Śuddhavidyā down to Air."
[The sequence] ending with Śakti resides in the seat of Vyoma (Space). Now, he describes the process of pervasion within the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā):

Earth ending with the element Bhūta, Water ending with the element Āpa, Fire ending with the element Śabda, the [seat of] Action ending with the organs of action (karmendriya), Wind ending with the intellect (buddhi), and Space ending with the intellect—these reside in the stone, that is, in the Brahma-stone.

It is easily understood through the method of explaining the pervasion of the *liṅga*. Regarding the sequence of the method for the deposition of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is as follows: the Guru, standing at the location of the feet, should begin the deposition of the principles and so forth; he should deposit the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) upon the *liṅga* with the syllable *sauḥ*.
Having relied upon the Śaktisūtra, which maintains that [the world] is produced by a cause, one should begin the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa):
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Soma, the lord of the principle of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Śakti; Oṃ hāṃ...
"Oṃ, obeisance to Dharman, the presiding deity of the Śakti-tattva"—thus in the portion for Rudra.
889) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the presiding deity of the Sadāśiva-tattva.

Salutation to Ajeśa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Īśvara (Īśvaratattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the four-faced one, the presiding lord of the principle of Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyātattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the presiding lord of the principle of Pure Knowledge.
Salutation to Kalyāṇa; thus for the portion of Viṣṇu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣāṇa, the lord of the principle of Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Kalā (kalā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ketudhvaja, the lord of the principle of Kalā.

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Time (kālatattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of Time, whose face is like a cresting flame (śikhivaktra). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Necessity (niyatitattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of Necessity, the Great Banner (mahādhvaja). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva).
Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the Principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva), Meghanirhrāda.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of Attachment (rāga-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the Principle of Attachment, Patravā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of Puruṣa. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Prakṛti. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Pitāmaha, the lord of the principle of Prakṛti. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Buddhi. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Buddha, the lord of the principle of Buddhi.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ahaṅkṛta, the lord of the principle of ego. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of mind (manas-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Saṅkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind.

p. 890) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the reality of the hearer (*śrotṛtattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vyomadharā, the sovereign of the state of being a hearer (*śrotṛtvādhipā*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the reality of the speaker (*tvattattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, [homage to] the speaker (*tvat*...).
Homage to the Lord of the Principle of All Limbs. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of the Eye.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prakāśa, the Lord of the Principle of the Eye. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of the Tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahāvaktra, the Lord of the Principle of the Tongue.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of smell (ghrāṇa-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viluṇḍaka, the lord of the element of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of speech (vāk-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dundubhi, the lord of the element of speech. Oṃ hāṃ...

Homage to Pāṇitatva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Samādāna, the lord of Pāṇitatvatattva. Oṃ hā, homage to Pādatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Caṅkramaṇa, the lord of Pādatattvatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pāyutattva. Oṃ hāṃ.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of air (pāyutatva), who has swift hands. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the generative organ (upasthatatva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ghanānanda, the Lord of the principle of the generative organ (upasthatatva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātṛtatva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātṛ).

Salutation to the subtle *nāda*, the presiding lord of that reality (*tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the reality of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Balavaktara, the presiding lord of the reality of the subtle element of touch. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to the principle of the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhānumat, the lord of the principle of the subtle element of form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jalada, the lord of the principle of the subtle element of taste.
p. 891) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātratattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandhakṣaya, the sovereign of the principle of the subtle element of smell. Oṃ hām.

Salutation to the principle of space (*ākāśa-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣma, the lord of the principle of space. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of wind (*vāyu-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the principle of wind. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of fire (*tejas-tattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Principle of Fire, the Master of Radiance. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Principle of Water. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Principle of Water, the Lord of Waters. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Principle of Earth. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Principle of Earth.
"Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha"—thus in the Brahma-portion. Alternatively:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the thirty-six principles (tattvas). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Rudras, the lords of the thirty-six principles. Thus one should perform the placement simultaneously.

Now, relying on the eightfold division (*aṣṭapakṣa*), he states that [the visualization] should be meditated upon individually even upon the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the stone, in order to reveal the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the eight forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Earth:
"In the eightfold division, however, the forms beginning with Earth are from the East to the Northeast. This is clearly understood.

He states another alternative view: "In the fivefold system, the directions are north, south, east, and west. The meaning of this is as follows: the earth, presided over by Brahmā and others beginning with Sadyojāta, is in the western direction; water [is in the north].
Having thus performed the placement: Vāyu presided over by the Brahmā Vāmadeva in the north; Agni presided over by the Brahmā Aghora in the south;
Vāyu presided over by the Brahmā Tatpuruṣa in the eastern direction;
and Ākāśa presided over by the Brahmā Īśāna in the northeast.
The meaning is that one should meditate [upon it].
Thus, on the linga, the pedestal, and the stone, [one should meditate upon] the form of each respective Lord of the Tattvas.

Having described the method for the visualization of the placement of Mūrtīśvara, he indicates that this same sequence is to be observed everywhere, even in the case of images, while pointing out the specific distinction: "In images as well, however, there is the placement of the three principles (*tattva*)."

This same entire procedure should also be observed for images of the dancing form (Nṛttamūrti) and others, as well as for images of Śiva, up to the knees, throat, and head. Regarding the specific placement of the three principles (tattvatrayanyāsa),
he says "certainly" (kintu) up to the knees, throat, and head.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) such that the *ātmatattva* extends to the knees, the *vidyātattva* to the throat, and the *śivatattva* to the crown of the head; the rest is all as previously described—this is the intended meaning. Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated that for an image, however, the conceptualization of the three *tattvas* is performed just as for a *liṅga*.

"One should know that what is called *ātman* extends to the knees and ends with *vidyā*, while that called *śiva* is situated up to the crown of the head; the remainder should be performed as before. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the installation of the door and the temple (*prāsāda*), the limit for the placement of the three principles (*tattva*) is as follows:

He states the distinction: there is pervasion over the door and the udumbara branches. Regarding that tripartite [division], having divided the door into three sections—beginning from the lower udumbara branch, the *ātmatattva* is in the lower section; above that, in the middle section, is the *vidyātattva*; and beginning from the upper udumbara branch...
The meaning is that one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva as all-pervasive in the upper section and then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Likewise, in the Jñānaratnāvalī: "But the Ātma-tattva [is to be placed] on the threshold, reaching as far as the Māyā-tattva."
Then, having deposited the *vidyātattva* up to the edge of the region on the two branches,
he likewise deposits the *śivatattva* starting from the upper *udumbara* fruit up to the end of *śakti*.

Having also divided the temple into three parts, one should contemplate and install the *ātmatattva* ending at the base (*jaṅghā*), the *vidyātattva* ending at the neck (*gala*), and the *śivatattva* ending at the crest (*cūḍā*) or the top of the head (*śira*).
Now, he states the specific rule regarding the installation of Gaurī and others:

In the installation of Gaurī and the others, one should place the power consisting of action upon the pedestal, and knowledge within the body; the remainder should be performed as in the case of the pedestal.

Regarding Gaurī and the others— here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), since fierce forms have been mentioned in every instance concerning the varieties of peaceful Śaktis— it is said that, having first performed the nyāsa of Kriyāśakti upon the pedestal (pīṭha) and having placed Jñānaśakti within the body (vigraha), the remainder [should be done].

One should perform the collection of ritual acts as one does for the *pīṭha* (seat). In these [sites], the previously mentioned forms (*mūrti*), the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśa*), and their powers (*śakti*) reside. Thus, in the *Kāmika*, it is said that the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva are located at the knees, the throat, and the head respectively; and Māyā...
The Guru should install the pervasive [mantra] ending with *deśa-śakti*.
Action, knowledge, and likewise will are considered the sovereigns of the three principles; they are Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, and Madotkaṭā.
Since the Dhātrī is manifold, one who presides over the forms (mūrtīśī) should be joined with them; therefore, one should install the forms.
In the installation consisting of the five forms, Vāmā and the others are considered the forms. (Thus, p.

Now, regarding the installation of the Mukhaliṅga: having prepared a nine-square grid on the pedestal, one should place the principle of Sadāśiva (Sadāśivatattva) in the center and Īśvara in the east;
one should place Vidyā and Māyā in the southeast, and Kāla in the south and southwest.
And when the wind reaches the north, a man feels passion for a woman who possesses self-restraint.
In the northeast direction from the *pradhāna*, one should place the five Brahmās in their respective quarters.

The meaning is clear regarding the installation of the three principles (*tattva*). Regarding the specific procedure for the conceptualization of the three principles, it is as before; however, within the circle (*vṛtta*), one should install the deity Sadāśiva.
And also the lords of the forms [of the deities] in their original forms.
This is easily understood through the application of the previously mentioned nyāsa rituals. Thus,

having specifically described the distinctions such as the nyāsa that serves as the seed for the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of each individual object— such as the *liṅga* and so forth— the [author proceeds] with respect to the temples, *liṅgas*, images, and other items to be installed.

He states a general rule in the form of a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), saying that because it applies equally to what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned, the specific ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and so forth must be performed as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*),
even in the case of images [made of materials] such as earth and the rest, beginning with these nine principles (*tattva*).
Having meditated upon the pervasion, the seed-syllable, and the name of Mūrti, Mūrtīśvara, and the others,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) everywhere according to their established forms.

Regarding the installation of the *mukhaliṅga* according to the nine principles (*navatattva*) and so forth, it is taught that the principles beginning with Sadāśiva should be deposited within the pedestal (*pīṭha*) prepared by the nine lamps; furthermore, the thirty-six principles, including the principle of Earth, are to be deposited as described above.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [it refers to] Mūrti, Mūrtīśvara, and so forth, who were previously enumerated as eightfold and fivefold; [this includes] the knowledge of the three principles (*tattva-traya*) on page 815.
Furthermore, there is a mutual integration of the powers of action through their causal relationship;

for in the absence of such mutual integration, there would be no reciprocal connection, and thus liberation and the liberated state could not achieve their joint activity through independent autonomy. This is the seed.

The seed-syllables, names, and coarse mantras, as well as the forms—the forms to be meditated upon for each respective deity—which will be described; because [the practitioner] lacks thorough knowledge of these forms, they do not ascend to the intellect. Therefore, [the deities] remain as they are, according to their actual state, as will be explained subsequently starting with the earth element.

Having meditated upon the *kīrama* and having correctly established it within the awakened consciousness (*budhi*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) even in all images, as well as in all objects to be consecrated such as the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), and the temple (*prāsāda*). This is because, in the absence of a thorough knowledge of these [elements], that very ritual placement would be impossible.

By this, it is indicated that the teacher’s thorough knowledge of the principles (*tattva*) of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) of the four quarters of the Śiva-āgamas is also a foundation for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Now,
in order to explain the knowledge of how things exist as previously stated, he describes the state of the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśa*), and so forth.
Established in their respective objects, such as earthness and so forth, are the [five] elements;
above the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), the two, Soma and Sūrya, are situated.

Above those two is the one called Dharma; Gaṇeśa and Śarva are also situated there. Rūpa (Form) is situated [there], as is Paśupati. Ugra is within the sphere of Ahaṃkāra (Ego). Rudra is to be understood as being right there, born from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra). And Bhīma is in the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra).
The abiding of the Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśas). The meaning of this is:
earth is established within the state of water, while the four [deities] beginning with Ambā abide each in their own respective domain.
Fire [is dissolved] in water, water in air, air in space, and so forth;

by this, the relationship of cause and effect among earth and the other elements should also be understood through their relationship as substratum and superstratum. The subtle form of space, namely the *tanmātra* of sound, exists at the summit.

The moon and the sun are established; above these two, the moon and the sun, is that which is called Dharma—the Self (ātman) whose name is Dharma, who consists of the form of sacrifices such as the Siddha and Jyotiṣṭoma. By the metaphorical identification of the action and the agent, the sacrificer himself possesses the nature of Dharma.

Thus he is established. By this, the establishment of the eight forms (*mūrti*) has also been stated. Now, the establishment of the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśa*), namely Śarva and the others, in Gaṇḍa and the other locations is clear in meaning. Having thus described the state of the lord of the forms for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), [the author now speaks] of those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).
He describes the stationing of the Mūrtīśas and the Vidyeśvaras:

"The Vidyeśvaras are to be known as established in the principle of Vidyā. The Vidyeśvaras are Ananta and the others. By this [are included] the eight Bhairavas, such as Kṣurikarman, Ektā, Asitāṅga, and so forth.

They too are indicated [by this], because they also abide in that very place. Now, according to the fivefold division: Puruṣa resides from the earth up to the individual soul (puruṣa); Brahmā resides from the earth up to Māyā; Rudra resides from the earth up to Vidyā; and Viṣṇu resides from the earth up to Vidyā.
Īśvara; Sādākhya [extends] from the earth (kṣmā) up to Nāda; Śakti [extends] from the earth up to Parā as its limit.

Furthermore, Śakti, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action, and which takes the form of Dhārikā and so forth, abides from the earth up to the limit of Parā—that is to say, from the element of earth up to the principle of Śiva.
